The revised Bloom taxonomy supplies an ordered ladder of cognitive objectives, while constructivist learning theory insists that knowledge is assembled by the learner rather than transmitted intact. Read together, they yield four sequenced stages, each pinned to a rising rung of the taxonomy and each equipped with a distinct AIGC entry point. The Learning stage handles knowledge input. Micro-lecture videos and interactive animations, generated with AIGC support, deliver foundational concepts in a form that keeps early extraneous demands low 38 . Comparable media designs in art and design programmes-augmented-reality frameworks for practice-based education 39 and animation-based problem-solving materials 40 -indicate that the delivery format itself carries part of the instructional burden. Instructor-student interaction here stays largely one-directional, and the output is judged by a recall-and-comprehension rubric. The Thinking stage lifts the target objective toward analysis: AI-driven problem scenarios prompt learners to interrogate what they have absorbed, forcing conceptual reconstruction rather than passive acceptance 1 . Assessment shifts to the quality of reasoning traces students leave behind. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 In the Applying stage, skill transfer takes over. Students turn to open-source animation software to realize concrete schemes, moving from understanding to execution 3 . The teacher's role becomes that of a troubleshooter, and deliverables are scored against technical fidelity and completion. The Creating stage sits at the apex of the ladder, where an AIGC co-creation platform hosts original animation projects 10 . Here human-machine collaboration is genuinely reciprocal, and originality, coherence, and expressive intent form the evaluation criteria. Figure 2 traces the full activity sequence and tool-embedding nodes across the four stages. The escalation across stages is deliberate rather than incidental. Learning targets recall and comprehension; Thinking moves to analysis; Applying demands transfer into production; and Creating asks for synthesis and original expression. Each stage also hands something forward, since the artefact and the competence produced at one stage become the entry condition for the next: a student who has already interrogated a script arrives at modelling with a plan rather than a blank scene. The four stages do not carry equal weight in assessment. Final work is judged against the Creating stage, while the earlier stages are assessed formatively, which keeps the evaluative emphasis on original output without leaving the preparatory work unmonitored 35 . Eligibility required current enrolment in the core animation curriculum and no prior exposure to structured AIGCbased instruction, since the intervention presumes a comparable starting point in generative-tool familiarity 3 . Two intact classes served as the sampling frame, and allocation was made at class level, one class being assigned at random to the experimental condition and the other to the control. Randomising whole classes respected existing timetables, a pragmatic choice common in classroom-based research 28 ; with only two clusters, however, it cannot equate the groups in the way individual randomisation would, so the design is quasi-experimental and any class-level difference remains confounded with condition. The study is educational rather than clinical: participants were healthy students, the intervention was instructional, and all outcomes were educational measures. Approval from the institutional review board was obtained, and every participant gave written informed consent before baseline testing. The experimental group received the AIGC-driven LTAC integrated animation instruction, whereas the control group followed conventional animation teaching built around demonstration and guided practice 38 . Baseline equivalence was examined beforehand on sex ratio, age, prior animation experience, cognitive load, and creative thinking pretest scores. Categorical variables were compared with 𝜒𝜒 2 tests and continuous ones with independent-samples t tests; none of the comparisons was significant at p < 0.05, which is consistent with baseline equivalence without establishing it 30 . Table 2 reports these comparisons. As Table 2 indicates, the two groups did not differ appreciably on any measured attribute before instruction. That similarity makes a preexisting-difference account less plausible for the effects reported later, though with two clusters it cannot exclude unmeasured class-level differences 23 . The intervention ran for twelve weeks at four class hours per week, forty-eight class hours in total, and the same instructor taught both groups so that delivery style was held constant. Cognitive load was captured with a subjective rating instrument that separates intrinsic, extraneous, and germane subscales and records each item on a nine-point Likert continuum. The single-item mental-effort rating introduced by Paas provided the response format 42 , while the item content of the three subscales followed the differentiated instrument of Leppink and colleagues, which recovers the three load types as distinct components 43 . Splitting the construct this way matters for the present design, since the hypothesised pathways treat the three loads as functionally distinct rather than interchangeable 34 . That version was developed for primary-school children, however, and neither its item content nor its norms suit animation undergraduates. The battery used here therefore followed the published Chinese adaptation in task format and scoring logic, with item stems revised for an adult sample and re-checked by translation and backtranslation. As Table 4 shows, every subscale held together well enough to justify treating its items as a coherent measure. The answer lies in how generative tools rearrange the flow of information reaching working memory. When an open-source text tool renders a script's structure visible, students no longer spend effort parsing formatting conventions or reconstructing narrative scaffolding by hand; that housekeeping is offloaded, and the presentation-driven demand that ordinarily clutters early learning thins out 37 . The same logic extends to redundancy. Conventional animation instruction often forces learners to process the same content through several channels at once-verbal explanation layered over manual sketching-whereas the generative pipeline lets each channel do distinct work, trimming the duplicated processing that inflates extraneous load 13 . Freed capacity does not simply vanish, though. Fig. 9 Heatmap of standardized path coefficients linking the three cognitive load dimensions to the four creative thinking facets, with color intensity encoding effect magnitude and direction. Fig. 8 Scatter plot of creative thinking composite scores against intrinsic cognitive load, overlaid with the fitted quadratic curve. The vertex falls at a moderate load value, approximately 5.9 on the ninepoint scale, which is the pattern an inverted-U association implies. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 The generative activities in the Thinking and Creating stages demand that students evaluate, curate, and reassemble machine output, which is exactly the kind of effortful schema-building that germane load names 23 . The selective response of the facets asks for a different explanation. Fluency and flexibility trade largely on retrieval speed and category switching, capacities that improve with practice in either condition, so it is unsurprising that they rose in both groups without a group difference 28 . Originality and elaboration depend instead on deeper transformation-combining remote associates, refining a concept until it holds together-and these operations draw on precisely the schema-building resources that germane load names 30 . On this reading the intervention did not make students think more; it changed the quality of thinking that the freed capacity could sustain, which is why the advantage concentrated in the two facets most sensitive to deep processing. The correlations in Fig. 7 sharpen that account. Fluency and flexibility hang together closely, as they should if both index the breadth of an initial search through memory, and their joint insensitivity to condition suggests that the generative toolchain did not simply accelerate idea retrieval. Originality and elaboration form a separate and more moderate pairing, and their weak association with fluency matters for interpretation: had originality risen only because students produced more responses, its correlation with fluency should have been considerably higher than the 0.41 observed. The same two-part structure has emerged from factor analyses of the Torrance battery, where fluency-driven and transformation-driven components separate rather than collapse into a single dimension 31 . Set against the long-run decline in originality and elaboration documented for large samples, the present result reads as a modest counterpoint, since the facets hardest to move historically are the ones this intervention moved 46 . Ulger's finding that creative training can lift divergent-thinking scores without touching problem-solving is a useful caution in the other direction: facet-level gains need not generalise to the wider construct 29 . The inverted-U finding for intrinsic load carries a caution that the earlier sections could only foreshadow. Too little intrinsic challenge leaves creative reasoning underpowered, while too much saturates working memory and crowds out the generative operations creativity needs 34 . The practical lesson is that intrinsic load should be tuned rather than minimised. A teacher designing an AIGC-supported animation task ought to calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range-demanding enough to engage, restrained enough to leave room for exploration-rather than assuming that easier is always better 12 . This tempers a common but simplistic reading of load theory, and it is among the more transferable takeaways here. Set against prior work, these results are largely consonant but not identical. Studies pairing design thinking with germane load in STEAM settings likewise found creativity gains routed through deep engagement, which aligns with the mediation reported above 30 . The divergence lies in specificity: earlier flipped-learning and projectbased interventions reported broad creative-thinking improvement without partitioning which facets responded, so their apparent whole-scale gains may have masked the facet-level selectivity observed here 28 . Measurement grain is the likeliest reason for the discrepancy, since aggregating creativity into a single score can hide exactly the discriminant pattern that makes a mechanism legible 20 . Three implications follow for theory. The first concerns the status of germane load. Cognitive load theory has increasingly treated germane load as a redistribution of resources rather than an independent source of demand 14 , and the mediation estimate reported here gives that reconceptualisation an empirical foothold in a creative domain: germane load acted on originality and elaboration not directly but through a deep-processing strategy, which is what a redistribution account predicts. The second concerns the shape of the intrinsic-load effect. A curvilinear relation is hard to reconcile with the standard prescription to minimise load, and it suggests that the prescription was always domain-bound, holding for schema acquisition but not for tasks whose value lies in exploration. The third concerns creativity theory. Because the four facets responded differently to one instructional manipulation, treating divergent thinking as a single latent ability discards information that a facet-level model retains-an argument the creativity literature has long made on psychometric grounds 31 and that an intervention study can now make on experimental ones. For practice, the findings translate into three design rules rather than a general endorsement of generative tools. Assign generative assistance to the parts of a task that consume attention without building competence-formatting, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 rendering, asset production-and keep it away from the parts where the struggle is the point. Make sure something recruits the freed capacity, because a lighter task is not automatically a more generative one; in the LTAC model the curation, evaluation, and reassembly demanded in the Thinking and Creating stages did that work. And calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range instead of smoothing it away. For animation programmes weighing curricular reform, an open-source toolchain can lower barriers to production while raising the ceiling on deep creative work, but only where the instructional design treats load as something to shape rather than merely shed 32 . That conditional is the substantive message for anyone hoping to scale generative tools across higher education in art and design 3 . items.abstract_text: The launch of U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds created an unusual allocation problem: 10 intermediaries offered nearly the same underlying exposure, yet their flows diverged sharply. This paper is a focused reanalysis of the fund-flow and Reddit panel introduced by [Shi, J., Z. Wang, D. Ding, Y. Wang, C. Xia, Q. Ding, and T. Lim, 2026, Who Gets the Flows? AI-Based Brand Visibility, Social Media Sentiment, and Capital Allocation in the U.S. Spot Bitcoin ETF Market, Mathematics, 14, 1959, https://doi.org/10.3390/math14111959]. It does not present the dataset, text measures, BrandScore or the baseline sentiment-by-visibility association as new. Instead, it asks what the established association reveals about the division between category demand and intermediary choice. The contribution consists of three interpretive emphases applied to estimates already reported by [Shi, J., Z. Wang, D. Ding, Y. Wang, C. Xia, Q. Ding, and T. Lim, 2026, Who Gets the Flows? AI-Based Brand Visibility, Social Media Sentiment, and Capital Allocation in the U.S. Spot Bitcoin ETF Market, Mathematics, 14, 1959, https://doi.org/10.3390/math14111959]: within-date differences across funds as evidence about allocation, asymmetry across the conditional flow distribution and variation across market states. The pairwise flow-sensitivity formulation makes the allocation interpretation explicit. In the previously reported two-way fixed-effects model, common daily shocks are absorbed and the sentiment-by-visibility coefficient is identified from differences in issuer visibility among funds facing the same Bitcoin news. The coefficient is positive, the direct visibility effect changes sign between large-redemption and large-creation states and the interaction appears less consistently during stressed markets. The Driscoll–Kraay and issuer-bootstrap checks apply to the baseline coefficient (2.930), not the two-way fixed-effects coefficient (3.802), for which those checks were not conducted. The evidence is thus an associative allocation regularity, not a causal social-media effect: differences in issuer visibility are consistent with different flows across financial wrappers conditional on common category sentiment.

reading.interpretation: This paper has explored how the algorithmic gaze of AI-driven surveillance systems has the potential to inflict interconnected harms that undermine the core purpose of education, a crisis which is now intensified by the rise of behavioural and mental health monitoring. The first of these is a harm to learning. Here, students might find themselves surrounded by systems designed to maximise engagement rather than help them develop genuine understanding, providing these students with easily processed, algorithmically curated content. This approach reduces the cognitive effort necessary for higher order thinking to occur. Curiosity is potentially stifled as students are moved away from challenging material toward what the system predicts they will consume most readily, creating passive information recipients instead of active learners. The psychological harms are equally troubling. Constant surveillance of intellectual output and behavioural patterns may result in an environment of paranoia, stress, and a fear of intellectual risk-taking. When students are aware that their keystrokes and online habits are being logged, they learn to self-censor. They might stop asking questions that can result in innovation. They might also avoid exploring divergent ideas that lead to intellectual and psychological growth. These behavioural monitoring strategies can be viewed as punishing students for normal adolescent behaviours and thought processes, limiting the curiosity and thoughtful exploration that schooling should instead be nurturing. analysis.discussion: This paper has explored how the algorithmic gaze of AI-driven surveillance systems has the potential to inflict interconnected harms that undermine the core purpose of education, a crisis which is now intensified by the rise of behavioural and mental health monitoring. The first of these is a harm to learning. Here, students might find themselves surrounded by systems designed to maximise engagement rather than help them develop genuine understanding, providing these students with easily processed, algorithmically curated content. This approach reduces the cognitive effort necessary for higher order thinking to occur. Curiosity is potentially stifled as students are moved away from challenging material toward what the system predicts they will consume most readily, creating passive information recipients instead of active learners. The psychological harms are equally troubling. Constant surveillance of intellectual output and behavioural patterns may result in an environment of paranoia, stress, and a fear of intellectual risk-taking. When students are aware that their keystrokes and online habits are being logged, they learn to self-censor. They might stop asking questions that can result in innovation. They might also avoid exploring divergent ideas that lead to intellectual and psychological growth. These behavioural monitoring strategies can be viewed as punishing students for normal adolescent behaviours and thought processes, limiting the curiosity and thoughtful exploration that schooling should instead be nurturing. This psychological burden is compounded by equity harms. Algorithms are not developed in a vacuum; rather, they are trained on historical data, and when these data reflect societal inequalities, the algorithms tend to replicate if not amplify them. These systems disproportionately mischaracterise and limit students from underserved backgrounds with worrisome consequences. Differently abled students are flagged for learning behaviours that are not considered the norm. Students in lowincome communities are labelled as at-risk based on behavioural and language cues that are misinterpreted. In this capacity, the algorithmic gaze does more than just predict student outcomes, it can potentially dictate them. It can cement existing privilege for some while imposing an artificial, data-driven ceiling on the capacity of others, thereby transforming education from a tool for social change into a technological mechanism for the reinforcement of societal inequalities. While the present work has attempted to offer an examination of the potential harms resulting from AI-driven surveillance, it comes with limitations which revolve around several issues. The first limitation is related to generalisability: the study only investigates three AI-driven surveillance tools, so the findings do not represent the broader range of surveillance technologies used in Australian K-12 schools. Additionally, the analysis focuses on product websites, marketing pages, customer stories, and support documentation which are produced by technology companies and are likely to present technologies favourably, which does not reflect how these systems are experienced in schools. Lastly, the study does not include empirical work with students, so while the paper can identify potential harms it cannot establish how students actually experience these technologies in situ. In order to develop a comprehensive understanding of the real-world implications of these surveillance tools, empirical research is necessary. One approach would be to examine the lived impacts of AI-driven surveillance tools on diverse populations, mapping how the socio-technical dimensions of these systems affect teaching and learning. As part of this process, one might examine the values that are implicated in the design and development of surveillance systems and how these values are reiterated in everyday school life. Another fruitful area of research would be to engage with Australian regulatory and policy analysis to examine how these instruments are designed, highlighting how surveillance is shaped not just by technology, but by laws, institutions, and public policy. Such research would provide the information required for parents, youth, and policy makers to make decisions that are ethical and equitable when it comes to the implementation of new technologies in the classroom.

items.abstract_text: BACKGROUND Artificial intelligence (AI) in gastrointestinal endoscopy has focused on computer-aided detection (CADe) for recognition errors; AI addressing endoscope motion, coverage, workflow, and skill – collectively kinematic analysis – has not been systematically synthesized. AIM To map kinematic AI evidence across eight predefined domains and assessed its quality relative to CADe and surgical AI. METHODS MEDLINE/PubMed, EMBASE-OVID, Cochrane, and IEEE Xplore were searched following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses checklist (CRD420261320279). Studies applying AI to kinematic data in gastrointestinal endoscopy were eligible. Risk of bias used Cochrane Risk of Bias 2, Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2, and PROBAST + AI; certainty of evidence used GRADE. RESULTS Fifty-eight studies were included. Evidence generation was asymmetric: (1) Randomized controlled trial ratio approximately 5:1 (> 40 vs 8); (2) Patient ratio approximately 4:1 (> 27000 vs approximately 6200); (3) Annual publication ratio approximately 12:1; and (4) ≥ 6 vs 0 regulatory approvals favoring diagnostic AI. Withdrawal speed monitoring and coverage/blind-spot mapping reached moderate GRADE certainty, but all 8 randomized controlled trials were from China and 6 of 8 used the ENDOANGEL platform. The remaining six domains have not reached moderate certainty: (1) Workflow recognition and skill assessment are approaching clinical readiness; and (2) Autonomous navigation, robotic control, simultaneous localization and mapping/three-dimensional reconstruction, and instrument tracking remain at the engineering stage. Comparison with surgical AI indicated that the gap reflects ecosystem-level factors – absence of open datasets, benchmarking challenges, and regulatory pathways for motion-acting AI – rather than technical immaturity. CONCLUSION Kinematic AI addresses exposure errors that CADe cannot correct and has shown additive benefit alongside CADe. Two domains are ready for geographically diverse validation; six remain at the engineering stage. Priorities are open datasets, benchmarking infrastructure, and dedicated regulatory pathways for motion-acting AI.

reading.methods: The study adopted quantitative bibliometric analysis and qualitative content analysis. It examined articles on the integration of generative AI technologies within the educational system, guided by learning theories. Studies identified through the Scopus and Web of Science database indexing platforms, using the Boolean strings "generative artificial intelligence" AND "education" AND "digital learning", yielded 637 articles; after removing duplicate records, 614 articles were obtained for the screening process. The search strategy was developed through an iterative review of keywords commonly used in generative AI and educational literature. The selected keywords were chosen because they broadly capture studies examining the incorporation of GenAI technologies across educational and digital learning environments. Data sets were reported as search results from the indexing databases as of April 25, 2025. The data are visualised and interpreted through a bibliometric analysis using the Biblioshiny application integrated with RStudio. Bibliometric analysis provided a visual overview of influential publications, prominent author contributions, most productive countries, and current trends and themes related to generative artificial intelligence technology in the educational context. analysis.methods: The study adopted quantitative bibliometric analysis and qualitative content analysis. It examined articles on the integration of generative AI technologies within the educational system, guided by learning theories. Studies identified through the Scopus and Web of Science database indexing platforms, using the Boolean strings "generative artificial intelligence" AND "education" AND "digital learning", yielded 637 articles; after removing duplicate records, 614 articles were obtained for the screening process. The search strategy was developed through an iterative review of keywords commonly used in generative AI and educational literature. The selected keywords were chosen because they broadly capture studies examining the incorporation of GenAI technologies across educational and digital learning environments. Data sets were reported as search results from the indexing databases as of April 25, 2025. The data are visualised and interpreted through a bibliometric analysis using the Biblioshiny application integrated with RStudio. Bibliometric analysis provided a visual overview of influential publications, prominent author contributions, most productive countries, and current trends and themes related to generative artificial intelligence technology in the educational context. A systematic review process guided by PRISMA 2020 as a reporting framework was undertaken to ensure transparent reporting of the study identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and selection processes, resulting in 163 articles selected for in-depth content analysis. To ensure methodological rigour and consistency, duplicate records were initially removed during the PRISMA process. The remaining studies underwent title and abstract screening based on the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Articles published in English that focus on generative AI integrations in the educational and professional fields are included in the study analysis. Articles in the categories of review, review articles, bibliometric and systematic reviews, book, book chapters, Editorial, letter, and notes are excluded from the analysis. Eligible studies were subsequently subjected to full-text assessment. Studies that focus on generative AI integrations and their impact explicitly across higher and K-12 education and the professional sector are included. Articles that have not explicitly focused on the educational applications of GenAI are excluded from the final analysis. The PRISMA 2020 checklist is provided as Supplementary Material to indicate the location of the information corresponding to the relevant reporting items in the manuscript. The corpus of 163 articles has been selected for indepth content analysis, as illustrated in the PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1 ). The inclusion/exclusion criteria for screening and eligibility assessment are presented separately in Tables 1 , 2 . The same criteria were applied to all the records retrieved to determine their relevance to the review objectives and to determine whether the generative AI was the focus of a substantive discussion in an educational context. A manual inductive qualitative content analysis approach was adopted, and data were extracted and analysed by a single researcher. The 163 articles were examined through iterative reading and coding with respect to the research objective, integration of theory-based models, and key findings. The first stage involved the development and creation of open descriptive codes through a series of analyses of the studies included and the constant comparison of the data across the studies. The coded data were then collected by educational contexts as described in the studies and reported in the larger categories of higher education, school education and professional learning environments according to conceptual similarities across studies. Based on the outcomes of this analysis, three thematic domains of the integration of GenAI were identified: GenAI adoption, GenAI in language learning, and GenAI ethical use. The thematic domains determined the structure of the next thematic analysis of the selected studies and encompassed the main themes identified in the studies on the integration of GenAI in education. In the case of RO3, the relationship between pedagogical practices reported and learning theories addressed in this review was analysed in an interpretative way. The learning theories were not pre-existing categories of coding of the included studies, but were found during the initial inductive coding. Rather, pedagogical features, learning activities, teaching strategies, and the engagement of learners reported in the selected studies were identified, and then the features of pedagogical characteristics were analysed in relation to the key points of the learning theories discussed in this review. The classifications are not to be regarded as the theories that the authors of the original study explicitly reported or adopted. The Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/feduc.2026. 1947867/full#supplementary-material

analysis.discussion: The synthesis findings presented in Table 4 emphasise thematic categorisations of 163 articles into three primary aspects: generative AI adoption in academic and self-learning environments (121 articles), generative AI language learning (32), and generative AI policies and ethical guidelines (10) . In each category, the article aggregation at the higher, school, and professional levels is described below in the appropriate sections. Thematic categorisation was based on the primary analytical focus of each study; accordingly, language learning also reported in the studies was classified into subthemes: AI-chatbot and outcome-driven education, teacher professional development, and instructional and teaching support. This overlap reflects the cross-cutting nature of language learning across different pedagogical and technological contexts rather than duplication of thematic analysis. As the primary analytical findings indicate, there is a strong emphasis on generative AI adoption in academic and self-learning environments (121 articles), with results reported in higher education (64 articles), school education (8 articles), and professional sessions (49 articles). Within higher education, the subthemes of generative AI adoption-pedagogical, technological, psychological and emotional dimensions-along with adaptive learning through chatbots and outcome-driven education, illustrate the various perspectives and key factors influencing the adoption of generative AI technologies among higher education students. As one of the collective perspectives, the findings highlight a paradigm shift in education, whereby the integration of technology into pedagogy has redirected the focus of the conventional learning process towards self-directed learning. Similar findings were emphasised within the profession section, where the educational stakeholders' perspectives on the adoption and influence of generative AI were highlighted in the themes of "generative AI adoption factors," "Teacher professional development," and "Instructional and teaching support". These themes highlight the pedagogical implications of generative AI technologies explored by teachers across education and other professional sectors. As the findings demonstrate, the adoption of generative AI technologies has amplified adaptive and selfdirected learning among higher education students and teachers, creating vital opportunities for enhanced learning and pedagogical innovation (Hsiao and Tang, 2025; Martínez-Carrera et al., 2025) . Generative technologies create opportunities for professionals across various streams, especially in the design, law, and organisational sectors, to pursue lifelong learning and upskilling in their domains (Morandini et al., 2023) . The study's results on the technology-acceptance model (TAM) and UTAUT primarily provide evidence of the perceptions of learners and educators, perceived usefulness, ease of use, behavioural intentions and willingness to use GenAI. Results are also helpful in understanding the conditions that support adoption and can be used to provide evidence of intentions towards the pedagogical use of learning, without emphasising pedagogical transformation (Kanont et al., 2024; Kavitha and Joshith 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Taufiq Hail et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024) . At the same time, it is worth noting that pedagogical or learning outcomes have been identified as pedagogical transformation in the studies that examined adaptive learning environments supported by GenAI, AI chatbots and outcome-oriented educational applications (Abdulayeva et al., 2025; Unal, 2024; Worthley et al., 2025) . As important findings, generative AI-integrated Chatbot features with specific subjective purposes have improved students' learning outcomes, opening the space for various exploratory measures with generative AI (Neumann et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025) . The automation of feedback reports, lesson preparation materials, and assessment features is a key functional capability of generative AI, encouraging the teaching community to explore it as an assistive tool for out-of-classroom activities ( Jere et al., 2024) . The advantages and disadvantages of pedagogical use of GenAI are explored in these studies, which offer complementary insights into the integration of GenAI into learning processes. Simply incorporating generative AI tools into pedagogy may not affect learners' critical and higher-order thinking, especially among students. The alignment of pedagogical and structural approaches in the integration of generative AI tools can be a factor in developing learners' higher-order thinking skills (Chen et al., 2025; Chu et al., 2025a; Jere et al., 2024; Kim and Kim, 2025) . This shows that the pedagogical value of GenAI is not about using GenAI, but about how teachers design learning experiences that involve it. Clearly articulating the connection between the application of GenAI and learning theories and pedagogical design is essential; technology acceptance does not equal educational effectiveness. Text-based generative pretrained transformer models and their educational applications are utilised by students and teachers for various academic purposes, primarily for language learning (Nevárez Montes and Elizondo-Garcia, 2025). As per the findings in Table 4 , language learning is emphasised as an important application of generative AI platforms (32 articles), with 22 articles from higher education, 2 from school education, and 8 that focus directly on educators. The findings further indicate that the effective use of generative AI technologies is evident among students in higher education, in schools, and in the teachers' community. The collective findings highlight a pattern commonly observed among higher education students (Alhajji et al., 2024; Rezai et al., 2024) and teaching communities (Moorhouse and Kohnke, 2024; Pando et al., 2025) . While language proficiency and its learning outcomes have been assessed among EFL students (Aini et al., 2024; Hellmich et al., 2024; Meniado et al., 2024) and EFL teachers (Urazbayeva et al., 2024; Yang and Markauskaite, 2025) , both groups reported positive improvements in language proficiency levels. The predominant use of text-based generative AI, particularly ChatGPT, is evident in themes of outcome-driven education and language learning within higher education, as well as in instructional support and language learning in the teaching profession. The Collective findings indicate that both groups perceive ChatGPT as an effective supportive tool and that it has shown improvements in English-language learning and language proficiency development among EFL learners (Meniado et al., 2024) and educators (Tafazoli, 2024) . Text-based content generation and analysis are considered the main functional uses of generative AI among students, educators, and legal professionals (Nevárez Montes and Elizondo-Garcia, 2025; Prakash and Nair, 2024) . The other generative AI features, such as code and image generation, are mainly explored by students from computer streams (Sun et al., 2024a) and by design professionals in their respective courses (Kim and Kim, 2025; Wang and Zhang, 2023) . Offloading the KV cache to host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) frees HBM space and raises concurrency, but the additional cache management and host-to-device (H2D) load overhead inflates inference latency, higher concurrency fails to translate into effective throughput. This mixed-methods study, which leaned towards a qualitative design (qualitative dominant), investigated these issues among adult learners at a university in Ghana.
reading.findings: The results showed universal access to smartphones (99%), while 71% had access to a laptop. Adult learners in this cross-sectional survey reported a generally positive appraisal of their DWB. Overall, the DWB mean score (M = 4.58, SD = 0.76) is above the scale midpoint, indicating a favourable orientation towards GenAI use, although some variation exists across the well-being domains. The mental subscale showed modestly positive cognitive and psychosocial gains (M = 4.09, SD = 1.12), with the strongest item endorsements for improved problem-solving (M=4.94, SD=1.49), increased productivity (M=4.42, SD=1.59), greater decisiveness (M = 4.42, SD = 1.48) and feeling more cheerful (M = 4.42, SD = 1.64). The emotional subscale also reflected positive outcomes (M = 4.51, SD = 1.29), driven by items such as increased interest in new things (M = 5.08, SD = 1.46) and clearer thinking (M = 4.60, SD = 1.61). Following reverse coding, the physical DWB subscale recorded the highest mean (M = 5.14, SD = 1.45), with all indicators (sleep, eating, aches, and reduced exercise) scoring above the neutral point (4.93 ≤ M ≤ 5.37). However, item-level frequencies indicate that this pattern was not uniform. While most respondents selected the disagreement options, a minority reported physical strain: 17.0% reported disturbed sleep, 10.9% reported changes in eating habits, 16.5% reported physical discomfort, and 16.5% reported reduced physical exercise. Thus, although the overall trend suggests limited physical strain, less than half of the sample still experienced some bodily effects associated with GenAI use. For QoL, the composite mean (M = 2.06, SD = 0.94) shows that adult learners reported some improvement in daily functioning, safety, control, activity engagement, and time efficiency (Table 3). The item means cluster between 2.25 and 2.58, for instance, control over daily activities (M = 2.58, SD = 0.54) and participation in enjoyable activities (M = 2.54, SD = 0.54). Nonetheless, the QoL findings should be interpreted with caution for two reasons. First, some items had fewer responses (n = 111–135). Second, the non-substantive options (i.e., “Does not apply” and “Do not know”) were excluded from scoring, so the observed mean reflects only substantive responses. reading.interpretation: The rise of GenAI technologies in educational settings extends beyond instructional implications but also has consequential psychological impacts on the user. As accurately captured by Christodoulou and Zembylas23, technology acceptance is not a clear-cut matter of positive or negative attitudes but involves complicated stories and changes in relationships that affect the views and experiences of users. The present study attempts to address the gap in current literature on the lack of a comprehensive focus and understanding of the consequences of GenAI use on the “human side” of diverse cohorts of adult learners, particularly within the African/Ghanaian Taken together, findings from both the quantitative and qualitative phases paint a similar picture of how adult learners in the study perceive their DWB and QoL when interacting with GenAI. In the two phases of the study, adult learners' engagement with GenAI is characterised by coexisting gains and strain and not just a uniformly positive or negative experience. In the quantitative phase, DWB mean score was slightly above the 7-point Likert scale midpoint, with a meaningful minority of respondents reporting physical strain, and the composite mean of QoL indicated only modest gains in some aspects of GenAI-supported learning. The qualitative phase of the study throws further light on the mixed results in the survey; collaborators reflected on both appreciation for GenAI’s efficiency and anxiety over its encroachment on human creativity and authenticity. analysis.discussion: The rise of GenAI technologies in educational settings extends beyond instructional implications but also has consequential psychological impacts on the user. As accurately captured by Christodoulou and Zembylas23, technology acceptance is not a clear-cut matter of positive or negative attitudes but involves complicated stories and changes in relationships that affect the views and experiences of users. The present study attempts to address the gap in current literature on the lack of a comprehensive focus and understanding of the consequences of GenAI use on the “human side” of diverse cohorts of adult learners, particularly within the African/Ghanaian Taken together, findings from both the quantitative and qualitative phases paint a similar picture of how adult learners in the study perceive their DWB and QoL when interacting with GenAI. In the two phases of the study, adult learners' engagement with GenAI is characterised by coexisting gains and strain and not just a uniformly positive or negative experience. In the quantitative phase, DWB mean score was slightly above the 7-point Likert scale midpoint, with a meaningful minority of respondents reporting physical strain, and the composite mean of QoL indicated only modest gains in some aspects of GenAI-supported learning. The qualitative phase of the study throws further light on the mixed results in the survey; collaborators reflected on both appreciation for GenAI’s efficiency and anxiety over its encroachment on human creativity and authenticity. Using the unified ecological framework as a lens to understand the reciprocal and dynamic interrelationships between individuals, digital platforms, physical spaces, and macro-level factors, both findings highlight that adult learners’ DWB is a function of these interrelated factors. First, results from the survey and storytelling reveal that adult learners are knowledgeable of digital tools (including GenAI tools such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, etc.) and, on average, possess digital skills and competencies which they use to interact meaningfully across several digital platforms (i.e. Google, learning management systems). Second, interaction on digital platforms occurs at multiple levels and at different physical places (e.g. home, school setting) for some purposeful outcomes. Positive outcomes through GenAI use reflect gains (manifested as strengths) whilst the negative experiences Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:37204 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78289-5 14 and outcomes create digital anxieties (afflictions). Third, GenAI use within the higher education context is constrained or limited by institutional-level factors (macro-level) such as policies on GenAI use, access to digital platforms and type of engagement. Thus, institutional factors mediate and shape adult learners' use of GenAI within this context. As such, adult learners' experiences of the extent to which their level of need and satisfaction is met through GenAI use reveal their state of well-being/wellness. Furthermore, both results highlight that within the higher education context, adult learners’ use of GenAI on a variety of digital platforms to perform academic and non-academic tasks is pervasive. Multiple digital connectivity at different places fosters a continuous cycle of constantly and actively creating and recreating their digital experiences, leading to cognitive and affective gains as well as embodied strains. Through such a process, they develop several coping systems which are mostly culturally embedded to counteract and adjust to the unpleasant physical afflictions. In sum, adult learners' digital well-being occurs through these nested multiple layers of influence (at the individual, meso and macro-levels), and is sustained by the powerful functionalities In addition, the results reveal that adult learners' positive gains with GenAI usage moderately influenced their cognitive, affective, and psychosocial well-being. For example, the qualitative arm of the study showed that adult learners appreciated the powerful functionalities of GenAI through enhanced efficiency in learning, but expressed psychological strain and apprehension. While it is true that GenAI tools like ChatGPT can enhance cognitive tasks, for instance, by making problem-solving activities easier, improving self-efficacy for task resolution and enhancing the quality and originality of solutions83, blind usage does not foster critical thinking and problem-solving, which are essential for academic and lifelong success15. Furthermore, the study found that some adult learners experienced minimal effects on their physical well-being as a result of GenAI usage, necessitating the development of self-adaptive coping mechanisms to alleviate the negative impacts of their digital experiences. Inferring from the unified ecological framework8, which illustrates a linkage between physical and digital domains influencing DWB when interacting with AI, the results imply that while GenAI usage may confer mental and emotional advantages, these are accompanied by modest but consistent reports of adverse bodily effects. Past studies have suggested that GenAI can reduce stress by streamlining tasks or creating a stress-free and emotionally supportive learning environment42,43,84, but excessive use of such technologies can lead to heightened anxiety, burnout, and sleep disturbance85. The physical place comprises different built and natural characteristics8. reading.interpretation: This study examined the association between generative AI dependence and medical students' clinical reasoning and tested whether critical thinking statistically accounted for part of this association. The results showed that generative AI dependence was negatively associated with critical thinking, whereas critical thinking was positively associated with clinical reasoning. After critical thinking was included, the direct association between generative AI dependence and clinical reasoning remained significant, suggesting that critical thinking accounted for only part of this association. AI literacy statistically moderated the negative association between generative AI dependence and critical thinking, but high AI literacy did not eliminate this negative association. Given that this study used an observational, three-wave time-lagged design and did not include baseline measures, the results can only reflect associations among variables rather than strict causal relationships; pre-existing individual differences, reverse or reciprocal associations, and unmeasured time-varying confounders cannot be ruled out. In addition, the outcome in this study was self-reported Clinical Reasoning as reflected by diagnostic thinking disposition, rather than objectively demonstrated clinical reasoning performance, diagnostic accuracy, or patient safety outcomes. In summary, this study suggests that medical education should focus on fostering calibrated AI use, critical thinking, and AI literacy, rather than simply restricting AI use; future intervention studies are still needed to verify whether such educational strategies can actually improve medical students' clinical reasoning.

analysis.methods: Data were collected through a questionnaire survey between February 2026 and June 2026. Before participant recruitment, the study was approved by the Rehabilitation and Nursing School of Hangzhou Polytechnic University (reference number:330104197703023321). Participants were primarily undergraduate medical students with experience in using generative AI. This study was conducted in medical schools in Zhejiang Province. Questionnaires were distributed through an online platform, and data were collected over three waves of time-lagged surveys. At T1, generative AI dependence, AI literacy, and demographics were measured. About four weeks later, critical thinking was measured at T2. Clinical reasoning was measured at T3 after another interval of approximately four weeks. Anonymous self-generated identification codes were used to link the responses from the three waves. No particular personal information, such as surnames, student IDs or contact details, was collected. Temporal distance can help reduce the common method bias of self-reported data collected at a single time. It also offered a more concrete timetable for the proposed path from AI dependence to critical thinking and then to clinical reasoning. However, a three-wave time-lagged design alone cannot establish causal relationships among generative AI dependence, critical thinking, and clinical reasoning. Because baseline levels of critical thinking and clinical reasoning were not measured at T1, the observed associations may also reflect pre-existing differences among students, reverse associations, or reciprocal associations. For example, students with weaker critical thinking or clinical reasoning foundations may be more inclined to depend on generative AI. Therefore, the temporal order of the questionnaires should not be interpreted as determining the direction of the relationship, and PROCESS Model 7 combined with time-separated observational data does not transform the analysis into a causal or longitudinal mediation model. Meanwhile, this study used a combination of convenience sampling and snowball sampling. Recruitment information was disseminated through the academic affairs platforms of medical schools, medical course learning groups, campus announcements, and student association channels, and was forwarded by participating students to medical students in the same grade. The inclusion criteria mainly targeted undergraduate medical students who had experience using generative AI and were able to complete the three-wave followup. Generative AI experience was defined as having used at least one generative AI system for medical learning within the past 6 months, at least once per month. Questionnaire samples were collected through multiple channels, and invalid samples were excluded based on response completeness and IP duplication. After eligibility and data-quality screening at T1, the longitudinal cohort contained 648 unique participants. The raw data files contained the same 648 unique identification codes at T1, T2, and T3. All 648 participants completed the three waves and were successfully matched using their anonymous selfgenerated identification codes. No unmatched identification codes, duplicate identification codes, or item-level missing values were present in the retained dataset. Thus, retention from T1 to T2 and from T2 to T3 was 100%, no participants were lost to follow-up after the T1 cohort was locked. The final analytical sample comprised 648 complete three-wave cases, and the valid response rate met social science research standards. Secondly, this study selected undergraduate medical students with experience using generative AI as the study population for two main reasons. First, medical students need to process large amounts of professional knowledge, case information, and evidence within limited study time. GenAI can substantially reduce the time and effort required for information searching and organization. Medical students therefore have a relatively strong need to use AI tools. Second, medical education requires students to move beyond knowledge acquisition toward clinical reasoning and professional judgment. If learners become overly dependent on AI-generated conclusions, the potential consequences may eventually extend to clinical competence and patient safety. Medical students therefore provide an appropriate population for examining the relationships among generative AI dependence, critical thinking, and clinical reasoning as reflected in self-reported diagnostic thinking disposition. Additionally, the current statistical analysis was based on 648 valid participants. Of these, 377 were female (58.2%) and 271 were male (41.8%). The numbers of students from the first to fifth academic years were 77, 139, 163, 160, and 109, respectively. Fourth-and fifth-year students accounted for 269 participants, or 41.5% of the sample. A total of 174 students (26.9%) reported having received formal AI-related training. GenAI use frequency ranged from "rarely" to "almost every day". Detailed sample characteristics are presented in Table 1 . Notably, in medical schools, years 1-2 corresponded predominantly to preclinical education, and years 3-5 corresponded predominantly to clinical education. Formal clinical reasoning instruction began in year 3, and clinical exposure increased progressively from year 3 to year 5. These contextual characteristics were considered when interpreting the findings and assessing generalizability. All core variables in the questionnaire were operationalized based on previous research. Scales originally developed in other languages underwent translation and back-translation. Researchers with backgrounds in medical education and English independently completed the translation and back-translation, and any discrepancies were resolved through discussion. For scales that already had validated Chinese versions or were developed specifically for Chinese medical students, the wording was adapted to the context of medical GenAI without altering the underlying construct. A questionnaire was developed and experts in medical education, psychometrics and AI education reviewed the items. A small-scale trial was also carried out to determine whether the wording is clear and feasible. The dimensions were emotional dependence, functional dependence, cognitive dependence and difficulty controlling AI use. They were modified to determine whether medical students were likely to use generative AI for information analysis, problemsolving and judgment-related tasks. The scale contained 18 items across three dimensions: open-mindedness, systematicity/analyticity, and truth-seeking. All items were scored on a five-point Likert scale. analysis.results: This study was grounded in cognitive offloading theory. It used a three-wave time-lagged survey of 648 valid responses. The analyses included hierarchical regression, bootstrap mediation testing, and moderated mediation testing with PROCESS Model 7. The study examined how generative AI dependence was associated with medical students' clinical reasoning through critical thinking. It also examined how AI literacy acted as a boundary condition in this cognitive transmission process. Five core conclusions were drawn. Specifically, there are five main findings, which stand in comparison with prior empirical studies. First, among medical students, the current findings reveal a significant negative association between generative AI dependence and clinical reasoning, as measured by the DTI. This does not mean that GenAI itself necessarily harms medical TABLE 9 Test of the moderated mediation effect. learning. Rather, it highlights the need to distinguish clearly between "use" and "dependence". Even after controlling for GenAI use frequency, AI dependence retained an independent negative association with clinical reasoning. This suggests that the educational risks of AI should not be judged only by how often students use it. More attention should be paid to whether students repeatedly outsource problem representation, evidence comparison, and final judgment to AI systems. Second, critical thinking may function as an important cognitive bridge between generative AI dependence and clinical reasoning. The current results show that greater AI dependence is associated with lower critical thinking, while critical thinking positively predicts clinical reasoning. This suggests that the risks of AI dependence may extend beyond general learning attitudes or cognitive preferences. This pattern is consistent with the theoretical possibility that reduced questioning, evidence verification, and consideration of alternative explanations may be associated with case judgment and diagnostic reasoning. These cognitive processes were not directly measured, and the outcome was self-reported diagnostic thinking disposition rather than observed clinical reasoning performance. The mediation result should therefore be read as a statistical pattern consistent with the proposed mechanism, not as process-level or performance-level evidence. Third, AI literacy statistically moderated the negative association between generative AI dependence and critical thinking. The association was strongest at low AI literacy (β = -0.528), weaker at the mean level (β = -0.361), and weakest at high AI literacy (β = -0.193). However, high AI literacy did not eliminate the negative association. These results are consistent with a statistical moderation pattern, not with the conclusion that increasing AI literacy would eliminate the association or that AI literacy is a demonstrated protective intervention. Even students with higher AI literacy may still miss learning opportunities if they routinely have AI perform higher-order thinking for them. Fourth, the moderated mediation results further show that AIrelated risks in medical education are shaped by the interaction of "user characteristics" and "patterns of use". Students with lower AI literacy showed a stronger negative association between AI dependence and critical thinking, which was in turn associated with lower clinical reasoning. Students with higher AI literacy are more likely to retain the information of verification and human supervision, thus reducing the negative indirect effect. Medical AI education should therefore focus less on tool proficiency and more on calibrated reliance and professional judgment. Fifth, in terms of the overall effect structure, AI literacy is positively correlated with both critical thinking and clinical reasoning, and it also moderates the negative path associated with AI dependence; thus, AI literacy extends beyond technical ability. It may reflect a type of "meta-technological ability" that helps students determine when to use AI, how to evaluate its output, and when human reasoning should be employed. As AI models continue to improve, this ability will be needed more. The more expert-like AI-generated answers become, the more students need to recognize when their own use is developing into inappropriate dependence. Taken together, these findings partially confirm, extend, and differ from previous research on active AI engagement, critical thinking, and potentially problematic AI use. Gerlich (9) reported that AI tool use was associated with cognitive offloading and critical thinking. Tian and Zhang (18) found that AI dependence was associated with lower critical thinking. The present study extends these findings by linking generative AI dependence to a professional outcome, clinical reasoning, through critical thinking. The findings differ from studies showing that LLM assistance can improve immediate diagnostic performance under structured conditions, such as Roemer et al. (4) and Brügge et al. (5) . Those studies mainly examined student-plus-AI performance, whereas the present study examined self-reported diagnostic thinking disposition without AI assistance. The findings are also consistent with Goh et al. (6) , which did not find that access to GPT-4 automatically improved physicians' diagnostic reasoning. Thus, the present results confirm some prior concerns, extend them to medical students and clinical reasoning, and differ from studies focused on immediate assisted performance.

analysis.limitations: This study has some limitations. First, although a time-lagged design was used to reduce common method bias, this study was not experimental and therefore cannot establish causal relationships. Future studies should use longitudinal observation, randomized trials, or instructional programs to examine the long-term associations between generative AI dependence and the development of clinical reasoning. Second, most of the sample consisted of medical students. Regional differences, institutional characteristics and other factors may limit the generalizability of these results to medical education. Future studies should determine whether similar findings generalize to learners in other fields, practicing clinicians, and healthcare training systems worldwide. Third, generative AI dependence, critical thinking, AI literacy, and clinical reasoning were all measured by self-report. Although the above measures have good reliability and validity, the observed associations may still be subject to social desirability and other biases. Future studies should combine self-reported data with case studies and standardized objective clinical examination (OSCE) scores and other performance indicators. Finally, generative AI is developing rapidly. Differences in model capabilities, interaction modes, and application settings may be associated with students' experiences and cognitive responses. However, the present study did not collect detailed information on which specific GenAI systems participants used or their purposes of use. Because different systems may involve different capabilities, interaction patterns, and levels of output reliability, the sample should not be assumed to be homogeneous with respect to AI exposure. This limits the generalizability of the findings and prevents us from examining whether the observed associations differ across specific GenAI tools or usage purposes. Future studies should therefore explore the differences among AI tools and specific types of medical learning tasks, and should collect detailed information on the types of GenAI systems used, the purposes and task contexts of use, and the frequency of use for each system. In addition, the CFA and subsequent hypothesis tests were conducted using the same analytical sample rather than an independent validation sample. Independent replication would provide a stronger test of measurement stability. The very high reliability coefficients for AI literacy and clinical reasoning, together with their relatively high mean inter-item correlations, also suggest that some item overlap may be present. Future studies should evaluate whether shorter forms can retain construct breadth while improving measurement efficiency.

Existing research mainly focuses on the macro-level technological empowerment of AI, yet insufficiently explores how healthcare organizations’ strategic commitment to AI translates into better medical service outcomes through individual psychological mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach From the perspective of human-AI collaboration, we utilize survey data collected from medical staff working in Chinese medical institutions to examine the mediating mechanisms and boundary conditions linking organizational AI orientation and AI value co-creation outcomes. Findings Drawing on social cognitive theory, the results reveal that healthcare organizations’ AI orientation is positively related to medical staff’s AI value co-creation outcomes, and AI self-efficacy mediates this relationship. Moreover, their creative self-efficacy positively moderates the relationship between AI self-efficacy and AI value co-creation. Originality/value This study clarifies the micro-level transmission paths between organizational AI orientation and medical staff’s value co-creation outcomes. It provides new insights for hospitals to enhance medical service quality and optimize human-AI collaboration during AI-driven healthcare organizational transformation.

analysis.methods: Fuzzy-Set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) has been widely utilised to identify strategy configurations across various fields, such as psychology (Cangialosi 2023) , sociology (Thomann 2020 ) and education (Sergis et al. 2018) . This method employs Boolean algebra to apply logical principles for comparing multiple cases (Fiss 2011; Ragin 2009) . Each case is depicted as a combination of several antecedents and an outcome, allowing these combinations to be compared and logically simplified through a bottom-up Boolean algebra process of paired comparison (Fiss 2011; Ragin 2009) . Therefore, this study chose to use fsQCA over Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) because fsQCA is used to (i) identify different combinations of conditions that are sufficient for an outcome (causal complexity) and (ii) identify and analyse how different factors interact and combine to produce specific results (configurational analysis). Beyond methodological advantages, fsQCA provides a theoryrelevant way to test our integrated framework because AIsupported SRL is characterized by causal complexity. fsQCA allows us to identify equifinal pathways (multiple sufficient routes to high SRL), synergistic effects (conditions that matter in combination rather than isolation), compensatory mechanisms (one condition offsetting the absence of another) and causal asymmetry (drivers of high SRL need not mirror drivers of low SRL). This configurational logic aligns with SRL theory's emphasis on dynamic, context-dependent regulation and helps interpret learner-AI interaction as multiple motivational-contextual routes rather than a single universal model. This analysis allows for the identification of complex causal configurations leading to high SRL, accommodating the interplay of multiple conditions. The study involved a total of 248 participants, comprising 163 females and 85 males, aged between 18 and 22 years (mean age = 19.2 years). Participants were undergraduate and graduate students from various fields of study, including computer science, finance, economics, art, foreign languages and business. To ensure relevance to the study, only those who had used AI tools in either self-directed or teacher-directed learning contexts at least once in the past 6 months were eligible. In this study, 'AI tools' refers to AI-enabled applications students used to support academic tasks (e.g., generative AI chatbots, AI writing assistants or AI-powered learning platforms). 'AI use' is operationalized as students' purposeful interaction with these tools to support learning activities (e.g., generating explanations/examples, drafting and revising, receiving feedback, summarizing, debugging or practice), including iterative prompting and evaluation of outputs when relevant to learning. Thus, AI use is conceptualized as a means through which SRL strategies are enacted, rather than a separate outcome in itself. Self-directed learning refers to the independent use of AI tools to support individual learning goals outside formal teaching environments. For instance, participants used AI tools to generate ideas, draft essays, complete language exercises or seek feedback on assignments. In contrast, teacher-directed learning refers to situations where AI tools were employed as part of classroom activities or assignments explicitly guided by instructors. Examples include the use of AI-powered educational platforms to complete course-related tasks, engage in collaborative projects or receive automated feedback in structured learning environments. Participants were recruited using a convenience sampling approach via university class announcements and online student forums. The invitation described the study purpose and eligibility criteria and included a survey link. The study protocol was approved by the institutional research ethics committee and informed consent was obtained prior to participation. A detailed demographic breakdown of the participants is provided in Table 1 . Data for this study was collected through a survey designed to measure UTAUT factors, SDT factors, perceived affordances of AI tools in learning contexts and SRL levels. The survey included validated scales for performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence and facilitating conditions (Venkatesh et al. 2003) , SDT factors (Chen et al. 2015) , perceived affordances (Al-Maawali 2020; Willermark and Islind 2022) and SRL (Broadbent et al. 2023) . The scales were adapted for AI-enhanced learning environments. In this study, 'AI tools' refers to learner-facing AI applications that students directly used to support academic learning tasks, including general-purpose generative AI systems (e.g., chatbots and writing assistants) and AI-enabled learning platforms that provide automated guidance or feedback (e.g., AI-supported tutoring/feedback functions). UTAUT constructs, such as performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence and facilitating conditions, were measured with 4, 4, 3 and 4 items, respectively. For the SDTrelated constructs, autonomy satisfaction, competence satisfaction and relatedness satisfaction were each assessed using 4 items. Perceived affordances of AI tools were measured with 5 items. Additionally, SRL constructs included academic self-efficacy (3 items), intrinsic motivation (4 items), extrinsic motivation (3 items), goal setting and time management (4 items), metacognition (4 items), effort regulation (4 items), social support (4 items) and task strategies (4 items). The full list of the questionnaire items used to measure each construct is provided in Appendix A. The SRL outcome was operationalized as a multidimensional indicator of overall self-regulated learning engagement. Consistent with the SRL-O framework (Broadbent et al. 2023) , the construct included eight dimensions: academic self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, goal setting and time management, metacognition, effort regulation, social support and task strategies. These dimensions capture complementary motivational, cognitive, behavioural and resource-management aspects of self-regulation. For analysis, item scores were averaged within each dimension and the dimension scores were subsequently combined to form an overall SRL score. The resulting composite reflects learners' overall capacity to regulate learning activities in AI-supported contexts rather than any single SRL process. The validity of the scales used in this study has been supported by extensive previous research, demonstrating their reliability and accuracy in measuring relevant constructs (Chen et al. 2015; Venkatesh et al. 2003) . The reliability of the scales was confirmed with Cronbach's alpha values ranging from 0.75 to 0.90, indicating acceptable to excellent internal consistency. The online survey was administered in April 2024 over a two-week period using a secure platform. Participants accessed the survey through a unique link to preserve anonymity and reduce duplicate responses. The survey platform did not allow submission with unanswered items; therefore, the final dataset contained no missing values on the analysed variables.

They also further highlight the critical role of perceived affordances as mediators and moderators, enhancing the relationships between innate psychological needs and external learning environments. This integrative approach provides valuable insights into the design and implementation of AI-supported SRL environments. We recommend designing the environments to foster autonomy and relatedness while also ensuring ease of use for learners. The final configurations are interpreted to derive insights into how different combinations of UTAUT, SDT and perceived affordance factors contribute to SRL outcomes. These findings inform the discussion on effective strategies for promoting SRL in AI-enhanced learning contexts.
analysis.discussion: To strengthen interpretation of the configurational solutions, we anchor each pathway in the mechanisms implied by the three theoretical lenses. From SDT perspective, autonomy, competence and relatedness satisfaction reflect motivational resources that shape the quality of regulation, ranging from more autonomous forms (intrinsic/identified) to more controlled forms (external/introjected). From a UTAUT perspective, performance expectancy and effort expectancy reflect largely instrumental value and perceived cost, while social influence reflects normative cues and facilitating conditions reflect contextual enabling resources. In AI-enhanced learning, high SRL may therefore emerge through multiple routes: some configurations reflect more agentic/autonomous engagement with AI tools, whereas others reflect more instrumentally or socially cued engagement that can still yield SRL when the tool is perceived as useful and the context provides adequate support. Importantly, these interpretations describe theorized mechanisms consistent with the solution patterns; they do not imply a single linear causal chain. A variable-centred SEM/regression approach typically estimates the net effect of each predictor on AI-SRL (e.g., whether performance expectancy or autonomy satisfaction has a positive average association). By contrast, our fsQCA results show equifinality (multiple sufficient pathways to high AI-SRL) and conjunctural causation (conditions matter in combination). For example, performance expectancy is meaningful in several pathways, but it is not uniformly sufficient by itself; its contribution depends on whether agency resources (e.g., autonomy/relatedness) or contextual supports (facilitating conditions) co-occur. Likewise, the high-coverage Solution 6b illustrates a compensatory pattern: strong facilitating conditions and relatedness can offset low effort expectancy. Such asymmetric and compensatory relations are often obscured when predictors are treated as independent additive effects. This is the added theoretical value of fsQCA for understanding learner-AI interaction. To move beyond listing solutions, we interpret configurations in terms of the psychological and behavioural mechanisms implied by SDT and UTAUT. In fsQCA, a configuration's practical importance is often reflected in coverage (how much of the outcome it accounts for) and its reliability in consistency (how consistently cases exhibiting the configuration show high AI-SRL). Accordingly, we interpret the highest-coverage pathway (Solution 6b; raw coverage = 0.357; consistency = 0.934) and then interpret theoretically salient pathways that feature SDT-based agency resources, including Solution 2b (raw coverage = 0.338; consistency = 0.929), which aligns with an autonomy-relatedness-value mechanism highlighted in prior motivation research. This study presents a nuanced analysis of the interplay between UTAUT and SDT factors in fostering SRL within AIenhanced educational environments. Through the application of fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA), we identified that autonomy satisfaction, relatedness satisfaction and performance expectancy are pivotal in promoting high levels of SRL. Our findings further elucidate the role of perceived affordances as significant mediators and moderators, amplifying the impact of these core factors. The integration of UTAUT and SDT frameworks provides a comprehensive theoretical model that captures the complexity of SRL processes. The configurational approach employed in this study reveals that no single factor is sufficient; rather, it is the combination of multiple interacting factors that leads to optimal learning outcomes. For practitioners, these insights emphasize the importance of designing AI tools that are not only functionally effective but also support learners' autonomy and relatedness. Institutions should prioritize creating an infrastructure that facilitates the seamless integration of these tools into the educational process, thereby fostering an environment conducive to self-regulation. While the study's cross-sectional design and reliance on self-reported measures present limitations, the findings provide a robust foundation for future research. Longitudinal studies and diverse educational contexts will be essential to further validate and expand upon these insights. Additionally, incorporating objective measures of SRL and AI tool usage will enhance the reliability of future studies.
analysis.limitations: Despite the valuable insights gained, several limitations should be noted, which also point to actionable directions for future research. First, our sample comprised learners who already had experience using AI tools in educational settings, which may constrain the generalizability of the findings to other populations and learning contexts. Future studies should replicate the analysis across diverse institutions, disciplines, educational levels and cultural/policy environments, where facilitating conditions and social influence may differ substantially. Second, the study relied on self-reported measures of SRL and AI tool use, which may introduce common-method bias. Future work should incorporate behavioural trace data (e.g., interaction logs, prompting iterations, time-on-task) and performance-based SRL indicators to triangulate learners' regulation processes beyond self-report. Third, because the design is cross-sectional, we do not test temporal ordering or dynamic reciprocal relations among perceived affordances, technology acceptance beliefs/contextual enablers, need satisfaction and SRL. Longitudinal or intensive longitudinal designs (e.g., weekly diaries, experience sampling) are needed to examine how these factors co-evolve across SRL phases (forethought-performance-reflection) during AI-supported learning. Fourth, while fsQCA is well-suited to identifying configurations (i.e., multiple sufficient pathways) and potential synergistic or compensatory mechanisms, the resulting solution patterns should be further validated using complementary methods. Future research could combine configurational approaches with SEM/regression to test hypothesized mediation/moderation processes (including the potential dual role of perceived affordances) and to examine the stability of findings through measurement invariance tests and calibration sensitivity analyses. Finally, intervention research is needed: experimental or quasi-experimental studies can evaluate whether targeted supports aligned with the identified pathways (e.g., agency-supportive AI activities, training and infrastructure for high-friction contexts and verification/ reflection scaffolds) can causally enhance AI-supported SRL and downstream learning outcomes.

Standards for the use of synthetic consumers should be established as soon as possible in response to validity disputes.
