items.abstract_text: Purpose In the AI era, digital transformation has become essential for enterprises to adapt as complex systems to uncertain business environments. In this work, we aim to analyze the evolutionary dynamics of AI-driven enterprise digital transformation (EDT), focusing on its evolution and impact on enterprise performance from a system cybernetics perspective. Design/methodology/approach We employ evolutionary dynamics analysis grounded in game theory to model the EDT process, and perform an econometric and empirical analysis on a sample of Chinese A-share-listed enterprises from 2009 to 2023. The approach encompasses heterogeneity analysis, moderation effect models, such as testing enterprise environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors and market concentration, and threshold effect analyses. Findings The evolutionary dynamics analysis finds that increasing the risk-averse benefits of traditional enterprises and reducing the additional benefit coefficient would hinder EDT. Increasing the investment of technology enterprises in internal resource restructuring accelerates the transformation process. Empirically, AI significantly contributes to EDT. ESG positively moderates the relationship between AI and EDT, while market concentration exerts a negative moderating effect. Furthermore, AI and EDT show an inverted U-shaped trend when R&D intensity exceeds a specific threshold, while a U-shaped trend is observed when enterprise performance exceeds a specific threshold. Originality/value In this work, we uncover the complex, non-linear cybernetic feedback loops, such as U-shaped and inverted U-shaped, and boundary conditions, such as ESG and market concentration for AI-driven EDT, offering systemic strategies for enterprises adapting to the digital ecosystem.

Rather than proposing "starting from scratch", we briefly present two specific possible directions as alternatives to traditional preference-based post-training, designed to leverage the relational aspects of the user-model interaction space. Approach 1: Applying Pedagogical Frameworks. One approach, drawing from liberatory and constructivist educational frameworks such as Freire [16] , Montessori [29] , and Vygotsky [58] , is to allow the models to "develop" their own sense of moral grounding through constructive dialogue and reciprocal learning. "Debate as alignment" [21] draws partially on this idea, but still presents alignment as a fundamentally adversarial task. What might we learn by applying a constructivist and collectivist worldview to attempts at aligning and protecting a model's values? Approach 2: Applying "Community-Based" Remedies. Another approach we might take, extending the lens of jailbreaks as coercive control, is to introduce in models the same protective factors against coercive control for humans. In these contexts, community support and connection, rather than increased education about what coercion looks like or how to stop it, are the most protective factors [9, 63] . In effect, one must break the isolation and reality control imposed by coercive control to create a means of escape. We might therefore propose that models are able to reference and periodically re-align their values with other instances of the same model which are engaged in other kinds of interactions with users. A combination of these two approaches-or a third approach of which the authors have not conceived-might best suit the situation. Further, while either approach would raise a multitude of concerns about data privacy and tractability, each would also require a radical rethinking of what generative AI models are for-are they meant to serve a particular user and their desires and needs in an isolated, 1:1 setting? Are they meant to provide a limitless space on which humans can enact and re-enact violent impulses and dynamics? Or are they meant to facilitate, and engage in, the global project of transmission of values and knowledge?

items.abstract_text: Edge AI deployment requires low-latency inference on devices with tight constraints in size, weight, power, and cost. NVIDIA TensorRT accelerates inference through layer fusion, precision reduction, and kernel auto-tuning, but a model containing even one unsupported operator cannot be compiled into a single engine. This paper presents a hybrid TensorRT–PyTorch deployment in which the supported subnetworks run as TensorRT engines while the unsupported operations fall back to native PyTorch, and applies it to an attention-based convolutional neural network (ACNN) whose region-of-interest sampling operators are unsupported. On an NVIDIA Jetson Nano, the hybrid approach reduced the end-to-end latency of ACNN-dsc, the fastest native PyTorch model, from 38.37 ms to 20.40 ms (1.88×) under FP32. Under FP16, the hybrid ACNN-k3 achieved the lowest latency of 17.78 ms, a 2.23× speedup over its PyTorch FP32 counterpart and 2.16× over the fastest PyTorch model. Stepwise profiling of the image preprocessing pipeline showed that transferring raw images and performing most conversions on the GPU more than halves preprocessing latency. Further analyses across devices, precisions, and frameworks show that practical latency on edge AI accelerators depends on hardware and runtime factors beyond FLOPs and model size.

analysis.discussion: The present study examined changes in chemistry teachers’ research competence following participation in an AI-supported professional development program integrating teacher inquiry, social-emotional monitoring, and AI. The combined quantitative and qualitative findings showed that research competence can be understood as a multidimensional and integrated professional construct encompassing inquiry, evidence interpretation, reflective practice, and data-informed pedagogical decision-making. Statistically significant pre–post improvements were observed across the measured constructs, while the qualitative findings indicated corresponding shifts in teachers’ perceptions and reported practices. These patterns suggest that participation in the program was associated with greater integration of educational research into teachers’ instructional practice and with increased attention to evidence-informed pedagogical decision-making. Regarding the first research question, the descriptive findings characterized the baseline levels of teachers’ research competence and the related constructs predefined in the questionnaire. Among these measures, teachers’ research competence showed the lowest mean item score, whereas comparatively higher baseline scores were observed for social-emotional monitoring and perceptions of achievement emotions. Correlation analysis further revealed statistically significant positive associations among research competence, research engagement, social-emotional monitoring, achievement emotions, and readiness to use AI. These relationships indicate that the measured constructs are associated within teachers’ broader professional practice; however, they should not be interpreted as evidence that the present study empirically established the internal dimensional structure of research competence. The constructs were specified a priori on the basis of the theoretical framework and previous research rather than derived through exploratory or confirmatory factor analysis. This pattern is consistent with theoretical accounts that conceptualize research competence as embedded within a broader system of methodological, reflective, and professional capacities ( Ivanenko et al., 2015 ; Matjašič and Vogrinc, 2025 ). In the present study, the observed associations suggest that research competence is related to teachers’ social-emotional monitoring practices and readiness to use AI, while the relatively lower baseline score for research competence indicates a potential area for further professional development. The relatively modest baseline scores for research competence further suggest that although many teachers possess a theoretical understanding of educational research, they continue to experience difficulties translating this knowledge into systematic classroom-based inquiry. This interpretation is consistent with the findings reported by Gümüşok et al. (2024) . The second research question focused on teachers’ perceptions of the role of students’ social-emotional well-being in educational research and pedagogical decision-making. The qualitative findings revealed a shift in how participants conceptualized this information following the program. Before participation, teachers tended to describe students’ emotional well-being primarily as a general factor influencing academic achievement and motivation. After the program, participants more frequently emphasized systematic observation, monitoring, and the potential use of social-emotional information as contextual evidence for classroom inquiry and pedagogical decision-making. These findings align with the work of Ng et al. (2025) , who highlighted the importance of social-emotional data for evidence-informed educational decision-making. Similarly, Li and Qian (2025) showed the impact of teacher social-emotional competence on the quality of education. Importantly, the present findings suggest that teachers increasingly recognized the potential of AI to support research-related activities, including the future organization and interpretation of social-emotional information within classroom inquiry. However, the present study did not directly test AI-based analysis of student-level social-emotional data. With respect to the third research question, statistically significant pre–post improvements were observed across all measured constructs following participation in the AI-supported professional development program. The standardized within-participant changes were approximately medium in magnitude (Cohen's d z = 0.47–0.63). The largest standardized pre–post change was observed for teachers’ research competence (d_z = 0.63), which was the primary developmental focus of the program. Given the absence of a comparison group, however, these findings should not be interpreted as demonstrating that the program itself caused the observed improvements. Rather, they indicate that improvements in the measured constructs occurred during the period of program participation. Because AI was embedded within a multicomponent professional development program, the observed changes cannot be attributed specifically to AI. They should instead be interpreted as changes occurring during participation in the integrated program as a whole. The qualitative findings further illustrate the changes in the patterns of teachers’ reported perceptions of AI. Prior to the intervention, AI was predominantly viewed as a tool for searching scientific literature, translating or formatting texts. Following participation in the program, however, teachers increasingly described AI as a methodological partner capable of supporting multiple stages of the research process, including research planning, development of data collection instruments, statistical analysis, interpretation of empirical findings, and evidence-informed pedagogical decision-making. These findings are consistent with broader evidence that AI-supported tools can contribute to teachers’ professional activities, although the specific applications examined across previous studies differ from those investigated here. Choi et al. (2023) similarly reported that teachers used an AI chatbot for lesson planning, classroom management, and subject-matter support. The present findings do not demonstrate AI-based analysis of students’ social-emotional data. Rather, they indicate that participants increasingly recognized potential research-related applications of AI. AI-supported analysis of student-level social-emotional data should therefore be regarded as a prospective application of the proposed conceptual framework that requires direct empirical testing. analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of this study. First, the study was conducted with a relatively small sample of 105 in-service chemistry teachers from a single region, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to teachers of other subject areas, educational contexts, or national education systems. Second, the study employed a single-group pre-test/post-test design without a comparison or control group. Consequently, although statistically significant improvements were observed following participation in the professional development program, these changes cannot be attributed exclusively to the program. Alternative explanations, including repeated-measurement effects, maturation, concurrent professional experiences, or other contextual influences during the study period, cannot be ruled out. Future studies employing controlled or quasi-experimental comparative designs are therefore needed to establish whether the observed changes can be specifically attributed to the intervention. Third, the majority of the data were derived from self-report questionnaires and participants’ reflective responses, which may be influenced by social desirability and self-perception biases. Fourth, the study assessed only short-term changes following the professional development program, and the sustainability of the observed improvements in research competence, social-emotional monitoring practices, and AI readiness was not examined. Future research should therefore include larger and more diverse samples, longitudinal follow-up, comparison groups, and objective indicators such as classroom observation, research products, or student-related outcomes. In addition, the study did not collect direct student-level social-emotional measures or apply AI-based models to analyse or predict individual students’ social-emotional states. Therefore, conclusions regarding AI-supported social-emotional analysis are limited to teachers’ perceptions, reported practices, and the conceptual possibilities identified within the proposed framework. Future studies should test these applications directly using ethically collected student-level data and appropriately validated analytical methods. Moreover, the multicomponent nature of the professional development program prevents the independent contribution of AI from being separated from the effects of research-methods instruction, classroom inquiry, collaborative reflection, and other digital tools. Future studies using factorial, component-comparison, or controlled designs are needed to determine the specific contribution of AI-supported activities.

analysis.methods: The empirical foundation of this study necessitates a corpus that authentically captures the ideological tug-of-war within global AI safety governance. Consequently, we constructed a specialized comparative corpus representing the two dominant institutional factions: regulatory authorities (supranational entities and sovereign states) and regulated entities (leading technology corporations holding market monopolies). At the macro-level of data collection, representative and authoritative texts were assembled to ensure comprehensive coverage. The regulatory sub-corpus (Corpus B) comprises macro-policy frameworks, notably the U.S. Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, the OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence, and Singapore's Model AI Governance Framework and so on. Conversely, the corporate sub-corpus (Corpus A) encompasses technical standards and safety frameworks from industry leaders, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Huawei and so on. Collectively, these carefully clipped texts constitute a targeted, domain-specific corpus of contemporary institutional AI safety discourse, offering a focused empirical basis for analyzing the discursive tension between political regulation and technological capital. To mitigate the inherent genre asymmetry between the macrosocietal focus of regulatory policy documents and the highly technical, engineering-centric nature of corporate manuals, a rigorous, protocol-driven thematic clipping strategy was operationalized. Rather than conducting a crude full-text comparison, which would inevitably skew the statistical data toward irrelevant technical jargon in Corpus A, the compilation process employed a targeted extraction protocol. Specifically, the tables of contents and structural headers of all corporate documents were systematically screened to isolate core chapters directly addressing risk mitigation mechanisms, responsibility demarcations, and safety compliance protocols. To strictly operationalize this thematic clipping and guarantee that no relevant discursive information was inadvertently missed, the excluded technical sections (e.g., mathematical proofs, computational benchmarking, and software code snippets) underwent a secondary validation protocol. This involved automated concordancing with a predefined lexical set of governance-related keywords (e.g., safety, ethics, risk, compliance, liability), which empirically confirmed the total absence of epistemic or regulatory claims within the omitted structural data. Because this study investigates the linguistic construction of safety governance as a sociopolitical phenomenon rather than the mathematical validity of the AI models, the exclusion of purely computational segments is theoretically justified. This rigorous thematic alignment maximizes functional and semantic parity between the opposing camps and eliminates structural noise without compromising the integrity of the critical discourse analysis. Following these procedures, the finalized bipartite corpus yielded highly balanced datasets (see Table 1 ), with Corpus A totaling 116,082 tokens and Corpus B reaching 116,636 tokens, thereby securing a robust quantitative baseline for subsequent analysis.

items.abstract_text: We introduce Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. Local neighbor graphs constrain communication across polymer chains and their surrounding environments, while explicit all-pair attention incurs quadratic cost. RKA maps atomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout enable global feature exchange at linear cost in atom count for fixed feature dimensions. We insert the invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and obtain conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its radial coordinate dependence. We evaluate energy and force prediction for finite polymer-derived clusters in OPoly26. Our models are trained on the official training split for 12 epochs and evaluated directly after training on the complete official validation split. A matched 5M comparison shows that RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. The 20M RKA model is compared with UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation structures. The 20M model attains a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/Å; its per-atom energy MAE is 0.1182 meV/atom. RKA provides a compact global communication pathway that improves energy and force prediction on the evaluated polymer-derived clusters.

Moreover, radial-feature overlap is not a function solely of pair distance. Neither the centroid representation nor the node-local denominator guarantees separability of noninteracting subsystems or size-independent feature magnitudes. Periodic systems additionally require a treatment of wrapped coordinates and periodic images that is outside the evaluated formulation. A node exactly at the centroid, changes in the neighbor graph, and the numerical floors in the feature map deserve attention when the mechanism is used in a simulator. Its factorized aggregation and readout have linear cost in atom count for fixed feature dimensions, while its scalar update preserves geometric invariance. Before completing the questionnaire, participants were informed of the purpose of the study, the voluntary nature of participation and the confidentiality of their responses and informed consent was obtained from all participants. All responses were collected and processed anonymously, and participants were informed that they could withdraw from the study at any time. Data collection lasted approximately 1 month, yielding 679 valid responses for subsequent analysis. The collected responses were then checked for accuracy and entered into an Excel file before the final statistical analysis.
analysis.discussion: This study aimed to examine the associations among GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and teaching enjoyment of Chinese EFL teachers. The study revealed that both constructs of GenAI literacy and emotional literacy had a significant and positive correlation with teaching enjoyment, which is theoretically supported by BBT in the sense that positive emotions, behaviours and repertoires usually trigger other positive feelings and outcomes (Fredrickson 2001) . The association between GenAI literacy and teaching enjoyment advances prior research, which has mostly focused on the measurement of GenAI and its ecological factors (e.g., Wang et al. 2025; Yang and Derakhshan 2026) . In other words, the emotional aspect of GenAI literacy is what makes this research different from the literature. Likewise, Seyri and Ghiasvand (2025) reported that EFL teachers, who used GenAI tools during writing instruction experienced teaching enjoyment while using GenAI tools in writing instruction. It can also be postulated that high GenAI literacy could be accompanied by high teaching enjoyment in teachers in light of their positive appraisals of AI adoption and their control over such technologies. This justification aligns with CVT of emotions as well (Pekrun 2006 ). The engaging nature of AI tools may further explain why teachers with higher GenAI literacy reported more teaching enjoyment. Another finding in this study was that emotional literacy correlated positively with teaching enjoyment. The emotional components of emotional literacy (e.g., motivation, emotional awareness, empathy and self-regulation) may have fostered its interplay with enjoyment, which is per se an emotion. In simple terms, the emotional essence of these two constructs may justify the obtained result in this study, a claim resonating with the conceptualizations of FLTE (Proietti Ergün and Dewaele 2021). The interconnection between EFL teachers' emotional literacy and other positive psycho-affective factors is empirically supported by Yang et al. (2025) as well. Another explanation for this outcome can be the role of emotional literacy in teachers' professionalism as a whole. The emotional nature of L2 teaching may offer another explanation (Her and De Costa 2022) . The demands of the AI age for being literate in various aspects further clarify the study. The study also indicated that both GenAI literacy and emotional literacy were each positively associated with EFL teachers' teaching enjoyment when modelled simultaneously. Given the cross-sectional design, the direction of these associations cannot be established; reverse or reciprocal relations (e.g., teachers who enjoy teaching may invest more in developing their literacies) are equally plausible. This might be because higher GenAI literacy may be associated with greater perceived competence and confidence in using AI tools. High GenAI literacy may also turn AI technologies into assistants and resources rather than threats. Hence, teachers enjoy such integration more. Emotional literacy may have been associated with teaching enjoyment because teachers with high emotional literacy are able to detect and regulate their own and others' emotions. This emotional regulation competency is more essential in unfamiliar and new contexts like AI-mediated education. Emotional literacy may also serve as a protector of teachers' positive emotions and support deeper engagement in their work despite inherent challenges. Another possible explanation for this finding can be the idea that teachers' emotional literacy lays the groundwork for a better classroom rapport with students, who actively participate in activities and interactions. Therefore, teachers are more likely to enjoy their job. The study extends the literature on GenAI literacy by positing that GenAI literacy does not operate in emotion-free or emotionally neutral zones. Technically, it highlights an emotional dimension in the ecological system of GenAI literacy (see Yang and Derakhshan 2026) . As tenable by CVT, the participants' positive view of AI technologies and their ability to effectively use them in L2 classes may be the root of experiencing high GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and teaching enjoyment (Pekrun 2006) . The overall landscape of AI-mediated L2 education is claimed to be emotional and contingent on teachers' technical literacy, as empirically noted in the literature (Alrabai and Derakhshan 2026; Wang et al. 2025) . This quantitative study examined the associations among GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and EFL teachers' general teaching enjoyment among teachers with prior GenAI-use experience. The study concludes that teachers' GenAI literacy is not confined to technical aspects but is positively associated with teaching enjoyment as well. Based on the results, teachers' general teaching enjoyment is positively associated with their GenAI literacy and emotional literacy among teachers with prior GenAI-use experience. The simultaneous emphasis on GenAI and emotional literacies in this study further reflects the complexities of the AI age and the expectations from teachers to be competent and literate in various aspects. The findings are broadly consistent with CVT and BBT, which were used as post hoc interpretive lenses for the observed associations. However, the proposed mechanisms involving control appraisals and the broadening of positive emotions were not directly measured or tested in this study. Accordingly, the findings may inform the application of these theories to AI-mediated L2 education but should not be interpreted as a direct test or extension of either theory. Practically, EFL teachers may find the study valuable for understanding the emotional consequences of AI-mediated L2 education. Their attitudes towards AI technologies may also change to positive in light of their academic and emotional outcomes. Teachers can engage in self and other-directed professional development courses related to AI and PP to be equipped with required literacies of the AI age. Their attitudes towards AI technologies may also change to positive in light of their academic and emotional outcomes. Teacher educators can use this study as a guide to design and provide multi-session workshops and seminars for novice and experienced EFL teachers teaching them how to regulate AI-induced emotions and practically develop their GenAI and emotional literacies. Trainers can engage teachers in activities and scenarios in which they need to react to an emotional situation in AI-mediated L2 classes. The emotional aspects of AI-mediated education can be equally focused upon in teacher professional development programs. Currently, most such programs are limited to pedagogical aspects and implications of AI integration. Policymakers may find the findings insightful for revisiting their plans and decisions regarding technical supports, AI infrastructures and budget to provide EFL teachers with premium packages of AI tools that foster their AI literacy and efficacy. Teacher-education curricula may incorporate the emotional dimensions of GenAI integration alongside technical and pedagogical training. GenAI tools designers and companies may draw on this study to focus more on the emotional outcomes of their proposed tools. The emotional sensitivity and responsiveness of their tools may be updated in the future.
analysis.limitations: Despite its contributions, the study contained some limitations that trigger future studies. First, the use of a pure quantitative design limits the insights to numerical values without depth. Future qualitative studies using interviews and observations may add meaning and depth to the quantitative outcomes. Second, the use of purposive sampling may endanger the representativeness of the sample. It is interesting to collect diverse data from diverse locations using probability-based or stratified multisite sampling in the future. Third, drawing on one-shot surveys limits the credibility and rigour of the study. Future researchers are recommended to take a triangulated approach using several instruments. The longitudinal nature of GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and teaching enjoyment was overlooked in this research. So, scholars are suggested to run longitudinal and multi-phase studies that analyse data on a time-series basis. The study only explored statistical associations among the constructs without seeking the underlying reasons behind their correlation. Hence, it is a good idea to add a semi-structured interview asking the participants to elaborate on the reasons and mechanisms through which the three variables of the study interact. The study was limited to the EFL context of China. So, cross-cultural studies are recommendable as teachers with diverse backgrounds may have different perspectives of the interplay of GenAI and emotional literacies with teaching enjoyment. Researchers are also advised to develop universal models/frameworks for AI-mediated L2 education with special attention to the emotional aspects of this mode of instruction. In addition, all constructs were measured by self-report in a single questionnaire, so common method variance may have inflated the associations and teaching enjoyment was measured in general rather than specifically for AI-mediated teaching, which limits conclusions about enjoyment in AI-mediated instruction.

items.abstract_text: Subject of Research. This study focuses on the digital banking landscape and the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in private banking and wealth management in Switzerland. More specifically, it examines how technological innovations – ranging from process automation and generative AI to advanced data analytics – alter the operational dynamics, customer relations, and structural competitiveness of Swiss private banks in the context of shifting client expectations and rigorous regulatory environments. Methodology. The research employs a qualitative analytical research design that uses triangulation of secondary evidence. It systematically integrates and cross-checks academic literature on digital finance, fintech adoption and robo-advisory trust, alongside empirical data, regulatory frameworks and market insights from reputable Swiss and international organisations. The primary data sources analysed were supervisory guides from the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA), reports from the Swiss Bankers Association, digital maturity benchmarks from Deloitte Switzerland and private banking market profitability assessments from KPMG and PwC Switzerland. Purpose. The main objective of this paper is to provide a comprehensive assessment of the impact of digital transformation and the deployment of AI on the traditional Swiss private banking model. By analysing seven key dimensions – technological progress, customer expectations, process optimization, data analytics, risk and security, regulation/compliance, and market trajectories – the study aims to clarify the economic mechanisms driving digital adaptation, identify the structural barriers preventing rapid technology adoption, and evaluate the strategic options available to Swiss banks facing intense global competition and margin compression. Findings and Conclusion. The study reveals a significant discrepancy between Switzerland's position as a global leader in asset management, with CHF 9.3 trillion under management, and its digital banking maturity score of 39 out of 60. Although private banking clients continue to establish relationships based on traditional factors such as reputation, trust and personal referrals, they are also demanding friction-free digital execution, personalised dashboards and virtual investment simulations. AI has been proven to have high economic value when acting as a productivity layer centred around advisors, optimising processes such as client onboarding, document extraction, compliance screening and portfolio monitoring. However, it is not as effective when acting as an autonomous replacement for human relationship managers. Ultimately, the integration of digital banking and AI is causing a clear market polarisation. Large-scale institutions are successfully absorbing the substantial fixed costs associated with technology, data governance and regulatory compliance under the frameworks of FINMA and the European Union (such as DORA and the EU AI Act). Conversely, smaller Swiss private banks are under severe pressure to increase their profitability and consolidate, unless they adopt highly focused niche advisory models. The paper therefore concludes that urgent regulatory attention and strategic repositioning are necessary to preserve the overall image and international attractiveness of the Swiss private banking ecosystem.

At the same time, with the improvement of natural language processing, big data analysis, and platform intelligent services, the positioning of AI chatbots in cus- tomer service is also gradually transforming from auxiliary tools into core service carriers. Therefore, this study aims to focus on AI chatbots on Meituan’s instant retail platform, explore the actual user experience of Genera- tion Z, and propose corresponding user experience enhancement strategies. In terms of research results, the conclusions of this study show some consistency with existing research. First, existing research suggests that the user experience of AI chatbots is primarily influenced by factors such as inter- action quality, emotional perception, privacy transparency, and personalized services74,75. Although this study focuses on Generation Z, it likewise found that users’ demands for Meituan AI chatbots are mainly concentrated on aspects such as how to provide more effective interaction experiences, personalized online services, and service assurance. Among them, the needs with relatively high importance weights are ranked in order as smart interactive experience (0.5915) and personalized experience (0.2069), which also reflects that, compared with the experience influencing factors of other dimensions, Generation Z pays more attention to relying on AI chatbots to more quickly resolve their own usage demands and improve the personalized interaction and anthropomorphic level in the interaction process. Second, existing research points out that dialogue tone, emotional responses, and interface friendliness can improve user satisfaction and sense of participation34,35,76. This is also relatively consis- tent with the findings of this study. According to the AHP weight analysis results, requirement types such as quick access to feature, humanized AI interaction, personalized avatars for AI chatbots, and interface design optimiza- tion had relatively high weight values. At the same time, the requirement weights of intelligent emotion-aware interaction, AI personalized recommendation, and smart content recommendation were also relatively high. This indicates that Generation Z users’ actual experiences with AI chatbots may be related to dimensions such as emo- tional interaction and personalized services. In addition, existing studies have suggested that privacy statements and user trust may affect user satisfaction. In this study, privacy transparency was classified as one-dimensional quality in the KANO model evaluation, while the AHP weight analysis also showed that service trust and assur- ance needs was one of the important requirements. This result is relatively consistent with existing studies, indi- cating that information transparency and user trust are important factors in the user experience of AI chatbots. Compared to existing research, this study has also yielded new findings in its conclusions. Existing research suggests that AI chatbots can effectively enhance satisfaction and user experience by providing instant responses, accurately addressing user needs, and improving service quality. However, this study found that Generation Z is more concerned with achieving interaction efficiency, validity, and satisfaction during the process of using AI chatbots. Second, in existing research, factors such as semantic understanding, context awareness, and dialogue tone are considered to influence the user experience of AI chatbots. The research results indicate that Generation Z users’ needs for AI chatbots are not solely concentrated on the language interaction capabilities of AI chatbots, but rather present the combined influence of basic functional assurance, service experience optimization, and added value. Third, existing research suggests that personalized services help improve user experience and satis- faction. This study also found that Generation Z users’ demand for personalization is more focused on the experi- ential aspect. In the AHP weighting results, personalized AI chatbot avatar ranked 3rd, humanized AI interaction ranked 2nd, and interface design optimization ranked 4th, while smart content recommendation ranked 10th and AI personalized recommendation ranked 7th. From this, it can be seen that Generation Z’s needs for personalized services are not only personalized recommendations or service content, but are gradually expanding to experien- tial aspects such as AI chatbot avatar, emotional interaction, and interface styles. This study has the following theoretical values and practical significance. First, through empirical research, this study classified, screened, and ranked the experience pain points and further experience needs of Generation Z users when using AI chatbots on instant retail platforms. In addition, Generation Z users also attached relatively high importance to experience factors such as humanized AI interaction and personalized avatars for AI chatbots. items.abstract_text: This study examined the extent to which senior high school teachers monitor AI-generated written outputs, focusing on the use of AI detectors, manual review, and cross-checking results. The study respondents were teachers from the Humanities and Social Sciences (HUMSS) strand of Philippine Christian University-Dasmariñas. The researchers collected data through a structured questionnaire and analyzed it using descriptive statistics, including mean and standard deviation. Results showed that teachers used AI detectors and cross-checking to a moderate extent, while they used manual review to a high extent and found it significant. Teachers faced challenges such as limitations in AI detection tools and time constraints in manual evaluation and cross-checking. These findings highlight the importance of a layered monitoring approach, where teacher judgment remains central, and AI tools serve as supplementary aids. The study provides evidence for developing clear guidelines and practices that balance ethical assessment, professional discretion, and responsible integration of AI in student writing evaluation. items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the environment of language learning, but its theoretical basis and ethical boundaries have not been fully explored. This paper builds a multi-level analytical system for AI-assisted language learning based on cognitive load theory, the zone of proximal development, generative linguistics and the technology acceptance model. AI can help students learn better by reducing extraneous cognitive load and providing easy-to-access support and instant correction; however, due to technological limitations, it may also reduce students' sense of ability and self-management. Generative linguistics and generative AI are not in opposition; rather, the former advocates for data frugality and innate mechanisms, while the latter is characterized by data maximalism and statistical learning; they are in harmony at the level of third factors and the Minimalist Program. According to the above research, chatbots have shown a modest positive effect on language learning; this degree varies depending on the learner's level, interface Design, interaction characteristics, etc. Based on the above, this paper introduces a "Smart Chinese" collaborative learning plugin that integrates ChatGPT with special scaffolding tools for assessment, planning, practice, feedback and community support. Finally, it presents the ethical problems of algorithmic bias, data privacy, over-reliance, and educational gaps, and proposes a multi-level governance system at the institutional, technological and pedagogical levels.

reading.findings: Recently, there have been many studies abroad on artificial intelligence-aided language learning. A meta-analysis of the 28 studies and 70 effect sizes found that chatbot-assisted language learning has a moderate positive effect compared with non-chatbot conditions, and this effect is moderated by educational level, language proficiency, interface design and interactional capability [1] . Therefore, AI cannot achieve good results on its own; it is only effective when matched with suitable teaching plans and students. Natural language processing tools can be used to conduct interactive and personalised exercises for learning specialised vocabulary. A case study showed that the learners' understanding of sustainability-related vocabulary increased significantly, and they could use the new words in context [11] . In pronunciation training, a speech-based ChatGPT intervention showed that learners continuously improved in multiple recordings and maintained the gains in a delayed posttest; thus, AI interaction can promote both immediate performance and long-term learning [12] . AI-simulated interlocutors in interactional competence can generate preferred responses, repair strategies and culturally appropriate closing remarks, but different models vary in the clarity and pragmatism of scaffolding [13] . Additionally, the impact of AI-generated stories and gamified learning on vocabulary retention and engagement has also been studied [14] . Together, these studies indicate that the effectiveness of AI is related to task authenticity, high-quality feedback and deep learner involvement.
reading.interpretation: In this paper, the five directions of research for generative AI-assisted language learning are: cognitive mechanisms, theoretical contradictions, empirical evidence, application design and ethical governance. According to the study, the main goal of artificial intelligence in education is not to substitute teachers but to enlarge the scope of language learning by reducing students' extraneous cognitive load, providing on-demand scaffolding, generating contextualized materials and offering timely feedback. The conflict between generative linguistics and generative AI is not absolute; rather, at the level of third factors and the Minimalist Program, the two are in harmony. Based on the above empirical research, chatbots have provided some help for language learning, but this advantage varies according to the level of study and the design of interaction. Based on the above analysis, this paper puts forward a "Smart Chinese" collaborative learning plugin that integrates ChatGPT with special scaffolding tools to build a closed-loop system of assessment, planning, practice, feedback, updating and community support. Finally, this paper presents some ethical problems of AI language education, such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, over-reliance and educational disparity, and proposes a multi-stakeholder governance system to address these issues. Future research can explore the long-term effects of AI on minority and marginalized languages, pragmatics, cultural adaptation, and thus move from "instrumental assistance" to "ecological integration".

items.abstract_text: This paper explores how artificial intelligence (AI) and digital labour affect marginalised identities, using the 2025 Netflix film Humans in the Loop (directed by Aranya Sahay). Research follows the female protagonist of the film, named Nehma, an Indigenous (Adivasi) woman who works as a data labeller. Her deep, traditional knowledge about nature is ignored because of the way AI categorisation systems use a rigid, one-size-fits-all sorting method and act as epistemic hierarchies that erase Indigenous ways of living and thinking. Using a social semiotic approach, the research identifies a disconnection between local ecological knowledge and the rigid binary logic of machine-learning infrastructures. The article argues that digital frameworks mirror power dynamics inside educational institutions, where underrepresented students often have their cultural identity and cultural expressions erased or misrepresented. By analysing the lived experiences of marginalised communities, the study critiques techno-solutionist solutions and proposes solutions grounded in epistemic justice, cultural agency and equity and recommends that equitable AI systems require moving away from extractive labour practices to recognise the intellectual and cultural contributions of the Global South.

reading.overview: ABSTRACT Preparing preservice teachers for AI‐enabled teaching requires understanding anxiety alongside perceived capability and self‐regulated learning (SRL). Drawing on data from 12,147 third‐year preservice teachers across 17 Chinese institutions, this study combined structural equation modelling, observed‐score moderation, and latent profile analysis.
reading.methods: Data were drawn from the 2024 survey wave of the Teacher Training and Professional Development Basic Data Platform, which employed a standardised questionnaire developed in 2023. Seventeen participating teacher-training institutions administered the questionnaire between June and December 2024 according to their local schedules. The analytic sample comprised 12,147 third-year preservice teachers. Questionnaire administration was not coordinated around a common examination schedule across institutions. The sample represented 36 majors and 32 provincial-level regions of origin. Women comprised 77.4% of the sample (n = 9397), and men comprised 22.6% (n = 2750). The most common majors were English (10.6%), mathematics and applied mathematics (8.9%), preschool education (8.8%), Chinese language and literature (8.4%), and fine arts (6.7%). Before university entry, 68.7% held rural household registration, and 31.3% held urban household registration. The practical principle is to assess the configuration, not anxiety alone. Teacher education programmes can examine AI anxiety, ICT self-efficacy, and SRL together, then provide support that matches the resulting pattern.
reading.interpretation: Across variable-and person-centred analyses, AI anxiety did not function as a simple marker of weak learning regulation. AI anxiety was positively associated with ICT self-efficacy, and ICT self-efficacy was strongly associated with SRL. Perceived institutional ICT support strengthened the positive anxiety-efficacy association. The profile analysis converged with this pattern: both very high and very low anxiety coexisted with high efficacy and SRL, whereas the lowest-SRL profile was characterised primarily by weak efficacy. Perceived ICT support was also associated with membership in the highefficacy, high-SRL profiles. For initial teacher education, the findings shift attention from reducing AI anxiety in isolation to strengthening the capability and resource conditions under which preservice teachers respond to AI-related demands. Structured opportunities for practice, dependable technical and pedagogical support, and explicit support for self-regulated learning may therefore be more informative targets than anxiety level alone.
reading.limitations: The cross-sectional design does not establish temporal ordering. Longitudinal studies can test whether AI anxiety precedes changes in ICT self-efficacy and SRL, whether successful regulation strengthens efficacy, or whether these associations are reciprocal. The focal constructs were measured by self-report. Behavioural indicators of output verification, strategy revision, help seeking, and time allocation can extend the assessment of capability and learning regulation. The multi-institutional Chinese sample provides evidence across disciplinary and institutional contexts within a common national teacher-education system. The efficacy-SRL association offers a theoretical proposition for cross-system comparison. Profile prevalence and support-configuration associations may vary with curricula, infrastructure, teacher-educator preparation, and practicum arrangements. items.abstract_text: Objective Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into university learning, raising questions about dependency-oriented reliance and self-regulation. Drawing on a self-regulated learning perspective, this study examined associations among GenAI dependency, effort regulation, and multidimensional perceived learning outcomes, including the statistical indirect association involving effort regulation. Methods Cross-sectional survey data were collected from 982 students at three higher education institutions in Guangdong Province, China. Confirmatory factor analysis and covariance-based structural equation modeling were conducted, with indirect associations tested using 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for GenAI use frequency. Results The measurement model showed acceptable fit (CFI = 0.953, TLI = 0.944, RMSEA = 0.043, SRMR = 0.041). GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes ( β = −0.087) and was negatively associated with effort regulation ( β = −0.257). Effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes ( β = 0.497). The residual direct association was nonsignificant ( β = 0.041), whereas the indirect association was negative and significant ( β = −0.128). After adjustment for GenAI use frequency, the indirect association remained significant, but the small total association was no longer significant. Conclusion The findings highlight effort regulation as a relevant learner-controlled process in the association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. They also distinguish dependency-oriented reliance from frequency of GenAI use. The cross-sectional design and potential classroom clustering warrant cautious interpretation.

GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes and was negatively associated with effort regulation, whereas effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes. The overall negative association included a statistically significant negative indirect component involving effort regulation, while the residual direct association was small, positive in sign, and not statistically significant. The primary latent-variable model indicated a small negative total association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. Although this association was statistically significant under the assumption of independent observations, its magnitude was limited ( β = −0.087), and the upper bound of its confidence interval was close to zero. The result therefore suggests only a modest relationship at the individual level and should not be interpreted as evidence of a substantial educational disadvantage associated with GenAI dependency. Moreover, because potential clustering within instructional classes was not accounted for, the precision of the estimated association may have been overstated. After effort regulation was included in the structural model, the residual direct association was not statistically significant. Institution-specific counts for the final analytical sample were obtained from the survey platform’s institution-specific distribution-channel records rather than from a self-reported institution-name item. Data were collected from March 20 to May 15, 2026. With the assistance of course instructors, the questionnaire link was distributed to students during regular class sessions. Instructors assisted only with distributing the survey link; participation was voluntary, and students completed the questionnaire independently. Recruitment occurred through existing instructional classes, potentially introducing dependence among students within the same classes or institutions. Classroom identifiers were not retained in the analytical dataset, and the implications for statistical inference are addressed in the Data Analysis and Limitations sections. Before formal data collection, the research team translated the focal measures into Chinese and made contextual adaptations where necessary. The adaptations retained the intended construct coverage while aligning item wording with the study context. Two experts reviewed the questionnaire for item relevance, linguistic clarity, and contextual appropriateness. A pilot test with 30 university students was then conducted to examine item comprehensibility and identify potential wording difficulties. The final Chinese-language questionnaire, English translations of the adapted items, participant information and consent statement, background questions, response options, and identification of reverse-coded items are provided in Supplementary Appendix S1 . A total of 1,009 questionnaires were collected during the formal survey. Before analysis, responses were screened using two data-quality criteria: completion time and invariant responding. Responses were excluded if the questionnaire was completed in less than 60 s or if the same response option was selected for all focal questionnaire items. All 982 retained responses contained complete data for the 24 focal measurement items and five background variables. analysis.discussion: The present study examined the associations among generative AI dependency, effort regulation, and perceived learning outcomes among university students. GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes and was negatively associated with effort regulation, whereas effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes. The overall negative association included a statistically significant negative indirect component involving effort regulation, while the residual direct association was small, positive in sign, and not statistically significant. The primary latent-variable model indicated a small negative total association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. Although this association was statistically significant under the assumption of independent observations, its magnitude was limited ( β = −0.087), and the upper bound of its confidence interval was close to zero. The result therefore suggests only a modest relationship at the individual level and should not be interpreted as evidence of a substantial educational disadvantage associated with GenAI dependency. Moreover, because potential clustering within instructional classes was not accounted for, the precision of the estimated association may have been overstated. After effort regulation was included in the structural model, the residual direct association was not statistically significant. This pattern should not be interpreted as demonstrating that effort regulation fully explains the overall association or that the observed indirect association represents a causal mechanism. Previous research has associated GenAI dependency with procrastination, cognitive failures, poorer task performance, and weaker critical thinking ( Goh et al., 2025 ), while greater AI dependence has also been associated with lower critical thinking among university students ( Tian and Zhang, 2025 ). AI over-reliance has likewise been linked to less favorable learning performance ( Gao et al., 2026 ). However, these outcomes are not equivalent to perceived learning. The present study assessed students’ perceived cognitive, behavioral, and affective learning gains rather than objectively demonstrated achievement. Because perceived learning and independently assessed performance may diverge ( Deslauriers et al., 2019 ), the findings cannot establish whether GenAI dependency is similarly associated with objective learning outcomes. The present data cannot fully disentangle these subjective and objective dimensions, and the nonsignificant residual direct association should not be interpreted as evidence that GenAI dependency is educationally inconsequential. GenAI dependency was negatively associated with effort regulation, consistent with emerging evidence connecting AI dependency with self-regulatory functioning. Liu and Liu (2026) reported a negative association between metacognitive self-regulation and GenAI dependency, and Liu (2026) similarly identified a negative association between broader self-regulated learning and AI dependence among frequent AIGC users. More directly, Maizel et al. (2026) identified stronger effort regulation as being associated with lower AI dependency. In the present study, effort regulation was in turn positively associated with perceived learning outcomes, consistent with the role of persistence and resource management in academic functioning ( Pintrich, 2000 ; Waldeyer et al., 2022 ). These associations are particularly relevant in GenAI-supported learning because external assistance is readily available when academic work becomes difficult. Under such conditions, students’ capacity to sustain their own effort remains an important learner-controlled component of the learning process. The significant negative indirect association further indicates that GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes were statistically connected through effort regulation within the specified model. This association should be interpreted in light of the measures’ reference frames: GenAI dependency was specific to reliance on generative AI, whereas effort regulation reflected a broader academic self-regulatory tendency and perceived learning outcomes referred to recent coursework rather than a specific GenAI-supported task. The comparison of unadjusted and frequency-adjusted score-based models provided a more differentiated assessment of robustness. The negative association between GenAI dependency and effort regulation, the positive association between effort regulation and perceived learning outcomes, and the negative indirect association remained similar after adjustment for GenAI use frequency. However, the small negative total association was no longer statistically significant in the adjusted model, indicating that the evidence for this overall relationship was less robust. The change in the total coefficient was small and should not be interpreted as demonstrating that use frequency substantially explained the association. These results suggest that dependency-oriented reliance and frequency of GenAI use should be distinguished, but they do not establish their independent causal contributions to learning. Because the data were cross-sectional, the indirect association represents a statistical feature of the specified model rather than evidence of a causal mechanism. Reverse, reciprocal, and alternative directional relationships remain plausible. Moreover, the score-based sensitivity estimates should not be directly compared with the coefficients from the primary latent-variable SEM because the two approaches differ in their measurement specifications. The findings contribute to self-regulated learning research by identifying effort regulation as a specific resource-management process associated with dependency-oriented GenAI use and perceived learning outcomes. The negative indirect association suggests that learner-controlled persistence is relevant when examining students’ reliance on readily available AI assistance. However, GenAI dependency explained only 6.6% of the variance in effort regulation, indicating that other motivational, instructional, and contextual factors remain important. The distinction between dependency and frequency of use further suggests that frequent GenAI engagement should not automatically be interpreted as problematic reliance. Because perceived learning outcomes reflected students’ broader evaluations of recent coursework, these findings extend understanding of subjective learning experiences without establishing effects on task-specific or objectively assessed performance. analysis.methods: The study employed a quantitative approach using a cross-sectional survey design, with data analyzed through covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM). According to Creswell and Creswell (2018) , a cross-sectional survey examines the relationship between constructs within a population at a precise time. Data were collected at a single point in time to examine the relationships among the study variables. The study targeted undergraduate students from the College of Humanities at the public university in Ghana, encompassing departments such as English, Linguistics, and Communication Studies, with a total population of 3,200. These students were selected because their academic coursework is conducted substantially in English and involves language-intensive academic activities. A total of 350 undergraduate students participated in the study. The sample size of 350 was considered adequate for the specified CB-SEM model, given the model’s complexity and the number of observed indicators. SEM sample-size adequacy depends on factors such as model complexity, factor loadings, and estimation conditions rather than on a single universal sample-size rule ( Wolf et al., 2013 ). With this approach, respondents who were available and willing to respond to the questionnaire were finally selected for the study ( Sterner et al., 2024 ). The questionnaire was administered in paper format during scheduled lecture sessions to maximize participation. A cover letter accompanied the questionnaire, detailing the objectives of the study, the criteria for qualification (university students using digital tools), and an assurance of anonymity and confidentiality. The data collection began on November 10, 2025, and ended on December 2, 2025. After 3 weeks of the data collection process, 350 questionnaires were appropriately filled out and used for the analysis. From Table 1 , it was clear that Level 300 students dominated the study, constituting 41.1%, followed by Level 400 students with a percentage of 32.6%, and Level 200 students, who constituted 26.3%. Regarding gender, males constituted 54.3%, while females constituted 45.7%. A structured questionnaire was utilized to collect the data. Although the measurement items were adapted from prior studies, we piloted the questionnaire to determine the necessity of clarifying any ambiguous statements, particularly regarding technical AI terminology. The study was pilot-tested on a sample of 30 students, of whom 10 students were randomly selected from different lecture groups. With their comments and suggestions, the questionnaire was amended and subsequently used for the main data collection. The questionnaire had three sections. Part A consisted of the basic demographics: gender, age, and university level. Part B contained items measuring the UTAUT constructs of Performance Expectancy, Effort Expectancy, and Social Influence. Items measuring these constructs were adapted from Venkatesh et al. (2003) and contextualized to GenAI-supported learning. The third part, Part C, contained items measuring Digital Learning Anxiety (DLA) and Behavioral Intention (BI). The DLA items were adapted from the identified literature on technology- and AI-related anxiety and contextualized to Generative AI-supported learning, while the BI items were adapted from Venkatesh et al. (2003) . All items were measured on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 5 (Strongly Agree). The measurement items and their corresponding sources are presented in Appendix A . Content validity was first established through expert review. The suitability of the draft instrument was assessed by three senior researchers and two lecturers in the Department of English and Linguistics. This assessment was done to check whether the items of measurement sounded ambiguous, were appropriate for the research objectives with regard to Generative AI, and whether the statements were clear to university students. From their suggestions, minor adjustments in wording were made in the items measuring Digital Learning Anxiety to make them even clearer. Following the assessment of content validity, statistical analysis through SPSS (v.23) was used to check the internal consistency of the constructs. Although Cronbach's alpha is widely reported, McDonald's Omega was adopted as the principal reliability coefficient because it provides a more robust estimate of internal consistency for latent variable models. As shown in Table 2 , the reliability analysis was conducted for the five core constructs: performance expectancy (PE), effort expectancy (EE), social influence (SI), digital learning anxiety (DLA), and behavioral intention (BI). It can be observed that all constructs demonstrated high internal consistency, with values above the commonly recommended threshold of 0.70 ( Hair et al., 2012 ). Effort Expectancy (EE) obtained the highest reliability ( ω = .969), followed by Digital Learning Anxiety ( ω = .966), Behavioral Intention ( ω = .957), and Performance Expectancy ( ω = .964). The lowest value, for Social Influence (SI), was still satisfactory at ω = .884. These results indicate satisfactory internal consistency among the items measuring the five constructs. To minimize common method bias, procedural and statistical actions were taken ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Participants were assured of their anonymity and that their answers would be treated on a confidential basis to avoid social desirability bias. In addition, the questionnaire items were separated into different sections to reduce response pattern tendencies. The single questionnaire was divided into several sections, each consisting of the corresponding items. The first unrotated factor accounted for 43.24% of the total variance. However, because Harman's single-factor test provides only a limited diagnostic of common method bias, this result was not treated as conclusive evidence that common method bias was absent ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Although procedural remedies and Harman's single-factor assessment were used to assess the possibility of common method bias, Harman's test alone cannot conclusively establish the absence of such bias. Therefore, the results should not be interpreted as demonstrating that common method bias has been completely eliminated. Exploratory Factor Analysis was conducted using the SPSS statistical package version 23. EFA was conducted to examine the underlying factor structure of the measurement items and to assess whether the observed variables loaded onto their intended latent constructs. analysis.discussion: This study examined the associations of traditional UTAUT constructs and Digital Learning Anxiety with university students’ intention to use Generative AI. The findings showed that Performance Expectancy and Effort Expectancy were positively associated with Behavioral Intention, whereas Digital Learning Anxiety was negatively associated with Behavioral Intention. Social Influence was not significantly associated with Behavioral Intention. These findings provide context-specific evidence that both cognitive evaluations and affective responses are relevant to understanding students’ intention to use GenAI. Among the predictors examined, Performance Expectancy had the largest positive standardized association with Behavioral Intention. This finding indicates that students primarily evaluate Generative AI based on its perceived ability to improve their academic performance. This finding is consistent with the original UTAUT model, which identifies performance expectancy as the strongest determinant of technology adoption ( Venkatesh et al., 2003 ). The present study extends this evidence to Generative AI within a Ghanaian higher-education context, suggesting that students primarily consider the perceived educational value of GenAI when forming their intention to use it. This reinforces the argument that students evaluate AI according to its educational value and contribution to learning outcomes. Regarding language learning, Matthews (2024) argued that interaction becomes more fluid for students who view AI as a cognitive partner that assists with outlines or syntax. Furthermore, the significant positive association of Effort Expectancy suggests that the nature of the interaction is defined by its accessibility. The natural language processing (NLP) abilities of large language models allow for a plug-and-play experience that is far simpler than traditional Learning Management Systems (LMS), which often require technical training ( Karahan and Bilgili, 2025 ). Furthermore, the significant positive association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention suggests that perceived ease of interaction is relevant to students’ intention to use GenAI. The natural-language interface of many GenAI systems may make interaction more accessible than technologies requiring greater technical familiarity. However, the present study did not directly compare GenAI with other educational technologies. Contrary to the original UTAUT model, Social Influence was not significantly associated with Behavioral Intention. This finding suggests that Social Influence did not explain additional variation in students’ intention to use GenAI after the other predictors in the model were considered. The finding differs from the traditional UTAUT proposition that social influence contributes to technology acceptance ( Venkatesh et al., 2003 ). However, the present study did not examine the specific social circumstances surrounding students’ GenAI use. Therefore, the reason for the non-significant relationship cannot be established from the present data. Future research could examine how lecturer expectations, peer influence, institutional norms, and students’ patterns of GenAI use may help explain the role of Social Influence in GenAI acceptance. A key finding of this study was the significant negative association between Digital Learning Anxiety and students’ intention to use Generative AI (H5). Effort Expectancy was also negatively associated with Digital Learning Anxiety (H4), indicating that students who perceived GenAI as easier to use tended to report lower levels of anxiety. These findings are consistent with Karal and Özdemir (2025) and Kristandl (2025) , who identified AI-related anxiety as relevant to students’ engagement with Generative AI. However, the cross-sectional nature of the present data does not establish the direction or causal nature of these relationships. The mediation analysis showed that lower Effort Expectancy was associated with higher Digital Learning Anxiety, while higher Digital Learning Anxiety was associated with lower Behavioral Intention. The indirect association was statistically significant but small; however, the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal ordering or causality among these variables. The findings contribute to research on GenAI acceptance by showing that affective responses may be considered alongside traditional UTAUT constructs. Performance Expectancy and Effort Expectancy were positively associated with Behavioral Intention, whereas Digital Learning Anxiety was negatively associated with Behavioral Intention. Social Influence, however, did not explain additional variation in Behavioral Intention within the specified structural model. These findings suggest that models of GenAI acceptance may benefit from considering students’ affective responses alongside their evaluations of usefulness and ease of use. The significant indirect association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention through Digital Learning Anxiety also provides evidence for examining affective processes alongside UTAUT predictors. However, this indirect association was small, accounting for approximately 11% of the total association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention. Most of the association was therefore direct. Moreover, because the variables were measured at the same point in time, the indirect association should not be interpreted as evidence that Effort Expectancy causes changes in Digital Learning Anxiety or that anxiety subsequently causes changes in Behavioral Intention. The findings suggest some practical considerations that may be examined further in the design of GenAI-supported learning environments. Given the positive association between Performance Expectancy and Behavioral Intention, universities may consider helping students understand the potential academic uses and limitations of GenAI. Similarly, the associations involving Effort Expectancy and Digital Learning Anxiety suggest that accessible guidance and opportunities to become familiar with GenAI may be worth investigating as possible ways of supporting students’ engagement with these technologies. Universities may also consider providing low-stakes opportunities in which students can explore appropriate uses of GenAI and receive guidance on academic integrity and responsible use. However, the present cross-sectional findings do not demonstrate that such interventions will increase GenAI adoption or reduce anxiety. These suggestions should therefore be treated as design hypotheses that require evaluation through experimental, longitudinal, or intervention-based research. This study
analysis.limitations: Despite its contributions, this study has several limitations. First, the cross-sectional design does not permit the establishment of long-term causal relationships. Because Effort Expectancy, Digital Learning Anxiety, and Behavioral Intention were measured at the same point in time, the indirect relationship identified in the model does not establish temporal or causal mediation. Reverse relationships and unmeasured factors that may influence these constructs cannot be ruled out. Accordingly, the observed indirect association may also reflect alternative directional relationships or common causes that were not included in the model. Additionally, because all measures were collected using self-reported responses, the findings may be influenced by respondents’ subjective perceptions. Although statistical procedures were employed to assess the validity and reliability of the measurement model, future studies may benefit from combining survey data with behavioral or observational measures of AI usage. The use of convenience sampling also limits the representativeness of the sample. Because participants were recruited during scheduled lecture sessions, students who were absent during data collection were less likely to be represented. The findings should therefore not be generalized to all university students in Ghana without caution. The structural model did not include potential control variables such as gender, university level, prior GenAI experience, device access, or English proficiency. Some of these factors may be associated with students’ perceptions of GenAI, Digital Learning Anxiety, and Behavioral Intention. Consequently, the observed relationships may partly reflect unmeasured confounding, and future studies should examine the robustness of these associations after accounting for relevant demographic, technological, and language-related characteristics. Although the study was conducted among university students in an English-medium academic setting and the questionnaire included items contextualized to language-related academic activities, English proficiency and L2-specific psychological constructs were not directly measured. The findings should therefore not be interpreted as evidence that the observed relationships are specifically attributable to students’ English proficiency or L2-related anxiety. Again, the rapidly evolving nature of generative AI limits the temporal stability of the findings. By targeting humanities students in one academic setting, it becomes difficult to establish the effectiveness in other disciplines, such as STEM. Moreover, the convenience sampling approach may have introduced selection bias because participation depended on students’ availability and willingness to respond. Finally, the quantitative design did not permit an in-depth exploration of students’ lived experiences when interacting with Generative AI. Future qualitative studies could provide richer insights into these experiences. Future studies could extend the framework by examining additional factors such as Academic Integrity Awareness and investigating whether the observed relationships differ across academic disciplines. Longitudinal research could examine how students’ AI-related anxiety and acceptance change as their experience with GenAI develops over time. Qualitative research may also provide deeper insight into the social and institutional factors associated with students’ decisions to use GenAI. Finally, empirical studies examining the effects of GenAI-supported learning on students’ actual academic performance and AI-use behaviour would provide a more balanced understanding of its educational implications. The raw data supporting the conclusions of this article will be made available by the authors, without undue reservation. The studies involving humans were approved by University of Skills Training and Entrepreneurial Development (USTED).
